Maximizing the number of qq-colorings

Po-Shen Loh ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544. E-mail: ploh@math.princeton.edu. Research supported in part by a Fannie and John Hertz Foundation Fellowship, an NSF Graduate Research Fellowship, and a Princeton Centennial Fellowship.    Oleg Pikhurko ††thanks: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA 15123. E-mail: pikhurko@andrew.cmu.edu. Research supported in part by NSF grant DMS-0758057.    Benny Sudakov ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, UCLA, Los Angeles, CA 90095. E-mail: bsudakov@math.ucla.edu. Research supported in part by NSF CAREER award DMS-0812005, and a USA-Israeli BSF grant.
Abstract

Let PG​(q)P_{G}(q) denote the number of proper qq-colorings of a graph GG. This function, called the chromatic polynomial of GG, was introduced by Birkhoff in 1912, who sought to attack the famous four-color problem by minimizing PG​(4)P_{G}(4) over all planar graphs GG. Since then, motivated by a variety of applications, much research was done on minimizing or maximizing PG​(q)P_{G}(q) over various families of graphs.

In this paper, we study an old problem of Linial and Wilf, to find the graphs with nn vertices and mm edges which maximize the number of qq-colorings. We provide the first approach which enables one to solve this problem for many nontrivial ranges of parameters. Using our machinery, we show that for each q≥4q\geq 4 and sufficiently large m<κq​n2m<\kappa_{q}n^{2} where κq≈1/(q​log⁡q)\kappa_{q}\approx 1/(q\log q), the extremal graphs are complete bipartite graphs minus the edges of a star, plus isolated vertices. Moreover, for q=3q=3, we establish the structure of optimal graphs for all large m≤n2/4m\leq n^{2}/4, confirming (in a stronger form) a conjecture of Lazebnik from 1989.

1 Introduction

The fundamental combinatorial problem of graph coloring is as ancient as the cartographer’s task of coloring a map without using the same color on neighboring regions. In the context of general graphs, we say that an assignment of a color to every vertex is a proper coloring if no two adjacent vertices receive the same color, and we say that a graph is qq-colorable it has a proper coloring using only at most qq different colors.

The problem of counting the number PG​(q)P_{G}(q) of qq-colorings of a given graph GG has been the focus of much research over the past century. Although it is already NP-hard even to determine whether this number is nonzero, the function PG​(q)P_{G}(q) itself has very interesting properties. PG​(q)P_{G}(q) was first introduced by Birkhoff [7], who proved that it is always a polynomial in qq. It is now called the chromatic polynomial of GG. Although PG​(q)P_{G}(q) has been studied for its own sake (e.g., Whitney [36] expressed its coefficients in terms of graph theoretic parameters), perhaps more interestingly there is a long history of diverse applications which has led researchers to minimize or maximize PG​(q)P_{G}(q) over various families of graphs. In fact, Birkhoff’s original motivation for investigating the chromatic polynomial was to use it to attack the famous four-color theorem. Indeed, one way to show that every planar graph is 4-colorable is to minimize PG​(4)P_{G}(4) over all planar GG, and show that the minimum is nonzero. In this direction Birkhoff [8] proved the tight lower bound PG​(q)≥q⁡(q−1)​(q−2)​(q−3)n−3P_{G}(q)\geq q(q-1)(q-2)(q-3)^{n-3} for all nn-vertex planar graphs GG when q≥5q\geq 5, later conjecturing with Lewis in [9] that it extended to q=4q=4 as well.

Linial [23] arrived at the problem of minimizing the chromatic polynomial from a completely different motivation. The worst-case computational complexity of determining whether a particular function f:V⁡(G)→ℝf:V(G)\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is a proper coloring (i.e., satisfies f⁡(x)≠f⁡(y)f(x)\neq f(y) for every pair of adjacent vertices xx and yy) is closely related to the number of acylic orientations of a graph, which equals |PG​(−1)||P_{G}(-1)|, obtained by substituting q=−1q=-1 into the formal polynomial expression of PG​(q)P_{G}(q). Lower bounding the worst-case complexity therefore corresponds to minimizing |PG​(−1)||P_{G}(-1)| over the family ℱn,m\mathcal{F}_{n,m} of graphs with nn vertices and mm edges. Linial showed that that surprisingly, for any n,mn,m there is a graph which simultaneously minimizes each |PG​(q)||P_{G}(q)| over ℱn,m\mathcal{F}_{n,m}, for every integer qq. This graph is simply a clique KkK_{k} with an additional vertex adjacent to ll vertices of the KkK_{k}, plus n−k−1n-k-1 isolated vertices, where k,lk,l are the unique integers satisfying m=(k2)+lm={k\choose 2}+l with k>l≥0k>l\geq 0. At the end of his paper, Linial posed the problem of maximizing PG​(q)P_{G}(q) over all graphs in ℱn,m\mathcal{F}_{n,m}.

Around the same time, Wilf arrived at exactly that maximization problem while analyzing the backtrack algorithm for finding a proper qq-coloring of a graph (see [6, 37]). Although this generated much interest in the problem, it was only solved in sporadic cases. The special case q=2q=2 was completely solved for all m,nm,n, by Lazebnik in [19]. For q≥3q\geq 3, the only pairs m,nm,n for which extremal graphs were known corresponded to the number of vertices and edges in the Turán graph Tr​(n)T_{r}(n), which is the complete rr-partite graph on nn vertices with all parts of size either ⌊n/r⌋\lfloor n/r\rfloor or ⌈n/r⌉\lceil n/r\rceil. In this vein, Lazebnik [21] proved that Tr​(n)T_{r}(n) is optimal for very large q=Ω⁡(n6)q=\Omega(n^{6}), and proved with Pikhurko and Woldar [22] that T2​(2​k)T_{2}(2k) is optimal when q=3q=3 and asymptotically optimal when q=4q=4.

Outside these isolated cases, very little was known for general m,nm,n. Although many upper and lower bounds for PG​(q)P_{G}(q) were proved by various researchers [11, 19, 20, 24], these bounds were widely separated. Even the q=3q=3 case resisted solution: twenty years ago, Lazebnik [19] conjectured that when m≤n2/4m\leq n^{2}/4, the nn-vertex graphs with mm edges which maximized the number of 3-colorings were complete bipartite graphs minus the edges of a star, plus isolated vertices. Only very recently, Simonelli [26] managed to make some progress on this conjecture, verifying it under the additional very strong assumption that all optimal graphs are already bipartite.

Perhaps part of the difficulty for general m,n,qm,n,q stems from the fact that the maximal graphs are substantially more complicated than the minimal graphs that Linial found. For number-theoretic reasons, it is essentially impossible to explicitly construct maximal graphs for general m,nm,n. Furthermore, even their coarse structure depends on the density mn2\frac{m}{n^{2}}. For example, when mn2\frac{m}{n^{2}} is small, the maximal graphs are roughly complete bipartite graphs, but after mn2>14\frac{m}{n^{2}}>\frac{1}{4}, the maximal graphs become tripartite. At the most extreme density, when m,nm,n correspond to the Turán graph Tq​(n)T_{q}(n), the unique maximal graph is obviously the complete qq-partite graph. Therefore, in order to tackle the general case of this problem, one must devise a unified approach that can handle all of the outcomes.

In this paper, we propose such an approach, developing the machinery that one might be able to use to determine the maximal graphs in many nontrivial ranges of m,nm,n. Our methodology can be roughly outlined as follows. We show, via Szemerédi’s Regularity Lemma, that the asymptotic solution to the problem reduces to a certain quadratically-constrained linear program in 2q2^{q} variables. For any given qq, this task can in principle be automated by a computer code that symbolically solves the optimization problem, although a more sophisticated approach was required to solve this for all qq. Our solutions to the optimization problem then give us the approximate structure of the maximal graphs. Finally, we use various local arguments, such as the so-called “stability” approach introduced by Simonovits [27], to refine their structure into precise results.

We successfully applied our machinery to solve the Linial-Wilf problem for many nontrivial ranges of m,nm,n, and q≥3q\geq 3. In particular, for q=3q=3, our results confirm a stronger form of Lazebnik’s conjecture when mm is large. In addition, for each q≥4q\geq 4 we show that for all densities mn2\frac{m}{n^{2}} up to approximately 1q​log⁡q\frac{1}{q\log q}, the extremal graphs are also complete bipartite graphs minus a star. In order to state our results precisely, we need the following definition.

Definition 1.1.

Let a≤ba\leq b be positive integers. We say that GG is a semi-complete subgraph of 𝐊𝐚,𝐛\boldsymbol{K_{a,b}} if the number of missing edges E⁡(Ka,b)∖E⁡(G)E(K_{a,b})\setminus E(G) is less than aa, and they form a star (i.e., they share a common endpoint vv which we call the center). If vv belongs to the larger side of Ka,bK_{a,b}, then we also say that GG is correctly oriented.

Define the constant κq=(log⁡(q/(q−1))log⁡q+log⁡qlog⁡(q/(q−1)))−2≈1q​log⁡q\kappa_{q}=\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log(q/(q-1))}{\log q}}+\sqrt{\frac{\log q}{\log(q/(q-1))}}\right)^{-2}\approx\frac{1}{q\log q}. All logarithms here and in the rest of the paper are in base e≈2.718e\approx 2.718. In the following theorems, we write o⁡(1)o(1) to represent a quantity that tends to zero as m,n→∞m,n\rightarrow\infty.

Theorem 1.2.

For every fixed integer q≥3q\geq 3, and any κ<κq\kappa<\kappa_{q}, the following holds for all sufficiently large m≤κ​n2m\leq\kappa n^{2}. Every nn-vertex graph with mm edges which maximizes the number of qq-colorings is a semi-complete subgraph (correctly oriented if q≥4q\geq 4) of some Ka,bK_{a,b}, plus isolated vertices, where a=(1+o⁡(1))​m⋅log⁡qq−1/log⁡qa=(1+o(1))\sqrt{m\cdot\log\frac{q}{q-1}/\log q} and b=(1+o⁡(1))​m⋅log⁡q/log⁡qq−1b=(1+o(1))\sqrt{m\cdot\log q/\log\frac{q}{q-1}}. The corresponding number of qq-colorings is qn​e(−c+o⁡(1))​mq^{n}e^{(-c+o(1))\sqrt{m}}, where c=2​log⁡qq−1​log⁡qc=2\sqrt{\log\frac{q}{q-1}\log q}.

Remark.  The part sizes of the maximal graphs above all have the ratio roughly log⁡q/log⁡qq−1\log q/\log\frac{q}{q-1}. The constant κq\kappa_{q} corresponds to the density m/n2m/n^{2} at which the number of isolated vertices becomes o⁡(n)o(n) in the optimal construction.

For 3 colors, we can push our argument further, beyond the density κ3\kappa_{3}. Now, due to the absence of isolated vertices, a rare exception occurs, which requires us to include an additional possibility. Here, a “pendant edge” means that a new vertex is added, along with a single edge between it and any other vertex in the graph. Proposition B.1 shows that this outcome is in fact necessary.

Theorem 1.3.

The following holds for all sufficiently large m≤n2/4m\leq n^{2}/4. Every nn-vertex graph with mm edges and the maximum number of 3-colorings is either (i) a semi-complete subgraph of some Ka,bK_{a,b}, plus isolated vertices if necessary, or (ii) a complete bipartite graph Ka,bK_{a,b} plus a pendant edge. Furthermore:

The corresponding number of colorings is 3n​e−(c+o⁡(1))​m3^{n}e^{-(c+o(1))\sqrt{m}}, where c=2​log⁡32⋅log⁡3c=2\sqrt{\log\frac{3}{2}\cdot\log 3}.

We also considered another conjecture of Lazebnik (see, e.g., [22]), that the Turán graphs Tr​(n)T_{r}(n) are always extremal when r≤qr\leq q. Building upon the techniques in [22] that answered the r=2,q=3r=2,q=3 case, we confirmed this conjecture for large nn and r=q−1r=q-1.

Theorem 1.4.

Fix an integer q≥4q\geq 4. For all sufficiently large nn, the Turán graph Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n) has more qq-colorings than any other graph with the same number of vertices and edges.

We close by mentioning some related work. Tomescu [28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35] and Dohmen [12, 13] considered the problem of maximizing or minimizing the number of qq-colorings of GG given some other parameters, such as chromatic number, connectedness, planarity, and girth. Wright [38] asymptotically determined the total number of qq-colored labeled nn-vertex graphs with mm edges, for the entire range of mm; this immediately gives an asymptotic approximation for the average value of PG​(q)P_{G}(q) over all labeled nn-vertex graphs with mm edges.

Graph coloring is also a special case of a homomorphism problem, and as we will discuss in our concluding remarks, our approach easily extends to that more general setting. Recall that a graph homomorphism ϕ:G→H\phi:G\rightarrow H is a map from the vertices of GG to those of HH, such that adjacent vertices in GG are mapped to adjacent vertices in HH. Thus, the number of qq-colorings of GG is precisely the number of homomorphisms from GG to KqK_{q}. Another interesting target graph HH is the two-vertex graph consisting of a single edge, plus a loop at one vertex. Then, the number of homomorphisms is precisely the number of independent sets in GG, and the problem of estimating that number given some partial information about GG is motivated by various questions in statistical physics and the theory of partially ordered sets. Alon [1] studied the maximum number of independent sets that a kk-regular graph of order nn can have, and Kahn [17, 18] considered this problem under the additional assumption that the kk-regular graph is bipartite. Galvin and Tetali [16] generalized the main result from [17] to arbitrary target graphs HH.

Another direction of related research was initiated by the question of Erdős and Rothschild (see Erdős [14, 15], Yuster [39], Alon, Balogh, Keevash, and Sudakov [2], Balogh [3], and others), about the maximum over all nn-vertex graphs of the number of qq-edge-colorings (not necessarily proper) that do not contain a monochromatic KrK_{r}-subgraph. Our method is somewhat similar to that in [2], and these two problems may be more deeply related than just a similarity in their formulations.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. The next section contains some definitions, and a formulation of the Szemerédi Regularity Lemma. In Section 3, we prove Theorems 3.2 and 3.3, which (asymptotically) reduce the general case of the problem to a quadratically constrained linear program. Then, in the next section we solve the relevant instances of the optimization problem to give approximate versions of our main theorems. Sections 5 and 6 refine these into the precise forms of Theorems 1.2 and 1.3. We prove Theorem 1.4 in Section 7. The final section contains some concluding remarks and open problems.

2 Preliminaries

The following (standard) asymptotic notation will be utilized extensively. For two functions f⁡(n)f(n) and g⁡(n)g(n), we write f⁡(n)=o⁡(g⁡(n))f(n)=o(g(n)) if limn→∞f⁡(n)/g⁡(n)=0\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}f(n)/g(n)=0, and f⁡(n)=O⁡(g⁡(n))f(n)=O(g(n)) or g⁡(n)=Ω⁡(f⁡(n))g(n)=\Omega(f(n)) if there exists a constant MM such that |f⁡(n)|≤M​|g⁡(n)||f(n)|\leq M|g(n)| for all sufficiently large nn. We also write f⁡(n)=Θ⁡(g⁡(n))f(n)=\Theta(g(n)) if both f⁡(n)=O⁡(g⁡(n))f(n)=O(g(n)) and f⁡(n)=Ω⁡(g⁡(n))f(n)=\Omega(g(n)) are satisfied.

We will use [q][q] to denote the set {1,2,…,q}\{1,2,\ldots,q\}, and 2[q]2^{[q]} to denote the collection of all of its subsets. As mentioned in the introduction, the Turán graph Tq​(n)T_{q}(n) is the complete rr-partite graph on nn vertices with all parts of size either ⌊n/r⌋\lfloor n/r\rfloor or ⌈n/r⌉\lceil n/r\rceil.

Given two graphs with the same number of vertices, their edit distance is the minimum number of edges that need to be added or deleted from one graph to make it isomorphic to the other. We say that two graphs are dd-close if their edit distance is at most dd.

The rest of this section is devoted to formulating the celebrated Szemerédi Regularity Lemma. This theorem roughly states that every graph, no matter how large, can be approximated by an object of bounded complexity, which corresponds to a union of a bounded number of random-looking graphs. To measure the randomness of an edge distribution, we use the following definition. Let the edge density d⁡(A,B)d(A,B) be the fraction e⁡(A,B)|A|​|B|\frac{e(A,B)}{|A||B|}, where e⁡(A,B)e(A,B) is the number of edges between AA and BB.

Definition 2.1.

A pair (X,Y)(X,Y) of disjoint subsets of a graph is ϵ\epsilon-regular if every pair of subsets X′⊂XX^{\prime}\subset X and Y′⊂YY^{\prime}\subset Y with |X′|≥ϵ​|X||X^{\prime}|\geq\epsilon|X| and |Y′|≥ϵ​|Y||Y^{\prime}|\geq\epsilon|Y| has |d⁡(X′,Y′)−d⁡(X,Y)|<ϵ|d(X^{\prime},Y^{\prime})-d(X,Y)|<\epsilon.

In this paper, we use the following convenient form of the Regularity Lemma, which is essentially Theorem IV.5.29′29^{\prime} in the textbook [10].

Theorem 2.2.

For every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there is a natural number M′=M′​(ϵ)M^{\prime}=M^{\prime}(\epsilon) such that every graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) has a partition V=⋃i=1MViV=\bigcup_{i=1}^{M}V_{i} with the following properties. The sizes of the vertex clusters ViV_{i} are as equal as possible (differing by at most 1), their number is between 1/ϵ≤M≤M′1/\epsilon\leq M\leq M^{\prime}, and all but at most ϵ​M2\epsilon M^{2} of the pairs (Vi,Vj)(V_{i},V_{j}) are ϵ\epsilon-regular.

3 Reduction to an optimization problem

In this section, we show that the solution of the following quadratically constrained linear11 1 Observe that the logarithms are merely constant multipliers for the variables αA\alpha_{A}. program answers our main problem asymptotically.

Optimization Problem 1.  Fix an integer q≥2q\geq 2 and a real parameter γ\gamma. Consider the following objective and constraint functions:

obj​(𝜶):=∑A≠∅αA​log⁡|A|;v​(𝜶):=∑A≠∅αA,e​(𝜶):=∑A∩B=∅αA​αB.\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}):=\sum_{A\neq\emptyset}\alpha_{A}\log|A|\,;\quad\quad\quad\text{\sc v}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}):=\sum_{A\neq\emptyset}\alpha_{A},\quad\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}):=\sum_{A\cap B=\emptyset}\alpha_{A}\alpha_{B}.

The vector 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} has 2q−12^{q}-1 coordinates αA∈ℝ\alpha_{A}\in\mathbb{R} indexed by the nonempty subsets A⊂[q]A\subset[q], and the sum in e​(𝜶)\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) runs over unordered pairs of disjoint sets {A,B}\{A,B\}. Let Feas​(γ)\text{\sc Feas}(\gamma) be the feasible set of vectors defined by the constraints 𝜶≥0{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\geq 0, v​(𝜶)=1\text{\sc v}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=1, and e​(𝜶)≥γ\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq\gamma. We seek to maximize obj​(𝜶)\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) over the set Feas​(γ)\text{\sc Feas}(\gamma), and we define opt​(γ)\text{\sc opt}(\gamma) to be this maximum value, which exists by compactness. We will write that the vector 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} solves opt​(γ)\text{\sc opt}(\gamma) when both 𝜶∈Feas​(γ){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\text{\sc Feas}(\gamma) and obj​(𝜶)=opt​(γ)\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\text{\sc opt}(\gamma).

Construction 1: Gα​(n)\boldsymbol{G_{\alpha}(n)}.  Let nn and mm be the desired numbers of vertices and edges, and let 𝜶∈Feas​(m/n2){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\text{\sc Feas}(m/n^{2}) be a feasible vector. Consider the following nn-vertex graph, which we call G𝜶​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n). Partition the vertices into (possibly empty) clusters VAV_{A} such that each |VA||V_{A}| differs from n​αAn\alpha_{A} by less than 1. For every pair of clusters (VA,VB)(V_{A},V_{B}) which is indexed by disjoint subsets, place a complete bipartite graph between the clusters.

Observe that any coloring that for each cluster VAV_{A} uses only colors from AA is a proper coloring. Therefore, if all n​αAn\alpha_{A} happened to be integers, then G𝜶​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n) would have at least ∏A|A|n​αA=eobj​(𝜶)​n\prod_{A}|A|^{n\alpha_{A}}=e^{\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})n} colorings, and also precisely e​(𝜶)​n2\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})n^{2} edges. Fortunately, the shortfall cannot be substantial:

Proposition 3.1.

The number of edges in any G𝛂​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n) differs from e​(𝛂)​n2\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})n^{2} by less than 2q​n2^{q}n. The proof is elementary and routine, so we will defer it to Section 3.4 so as not to interrupt this exposition. To recover from the O⁡(n)O(n) edge deficit, we extend the construction in the following way.

Construction 2: Gα′​(n)\boldsymbol{G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\prime}(n)}.  Let nn and mm be the desired numbers of vertices and edges, and let 𝜶∈Feas​(m/n2){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\text{\sc Feas}(m/n^{2}) be a feasible vector. If G𝜶​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n) from Construction 1 already has at least mm edges, then set G𝜶′​(n)=G𝜶​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\prime}(n)=G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n).

Otherwise, G𝜶​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n) is short by, say, kk edges, and k=O⁡(n)k=O(n) by Proposition 3.1. Let VAV_{A} be its largest cluster whose index AA is not a singleton. Suppose first that |VA|≥2​⌈k⌉|V_{A}|\geq 2\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil. 3.1 Structure of asymptotic argument

We are now ready to state our theorem, which shows that solutions to Optimization Problem 1 produce graphs which asymptotically maximize the number of qq-colorings.

Theorem 3.2.

For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, the following holds for any sufficiently large nn, and any mm less than or equal to the number of edges in the Turán graph Tq​(n)T_{q}(n).

(i)

Every nn-vertex graph with mm edges has fewer than e(opt​(m/n2)+ϵ)​ne^{(\text{\sc opt}(m/n^{2})+\epsilon)n} proper qq-colorings.

(ii)

Any 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} which solves opt​(m/n2)\text{\sc opt}(m/n^{2}) yields a graph G𝜶′​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\prime}(n) via Construction 2 which has at least mm edges and more than e(opt​(m/n2)−ϵ)​ne^{(\text{\sc opt}(m/n^{2})-\epsilon)n} proper qq-colorings.

Remark.  The number of colorings can only increase when edges are deleted, so one may take an arbitrary mm-edge subgraph of G𝜶′​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\prime}(n) if one requires a graph with exactly mm edges.

The key ingredient in the proof of Theorem 3.2 is Szemerédi’s Regularity Lemma. Part (ii) is routine, and full details are given in Section 3.4. On the other hand, the argument for part (i) is more involved, so we highlight its structure here so that the reader does not get lost in the details. The proof breaks into the following claims.

Claim 1.

For any δ>0\delta>0, there exists n0n_{0} such that the following holds for any graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) with n>n0n>n_{0} vertices and mm edges. The Regularity Lemma gives a special partition of the vertex set into V1V_{1}, …, VMV_{M} of almost equal size, where MM is upper bounded by a constant depending only on δ\delta. Then, we may delete at most δ​n2\delta n^{2} edges of GG in such a way that the resulting graph G′G^{\prime} has the following properties.

(i)

Each G′​[Vi]G^{\prime}[V_{i}] spans no edges.

(ii)

If G′G^{\prime} has any edges at all between two parts ViV_{i} and VjV_{j}, then in fact it has an edge between every pair of subsets U⊂ViU\subset V_{i}, W⊂VjW\subset V_{j} with |U|≥δ​|Vi||U|\geq\delta|V_{i}| and W≥δ​|Vj|W\geq\delta|V_{j}|.

Note that since G′G^{\prime} is a subgraph of GG, the number of qq-colorings can only increase.

Claim 2.

Let 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} be the set of colorings of G′G^{\prime}. Then, if we keep only those colorings 𝒞2⊂𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{2}\subset\mathcal{C}_{1} with the property that in each ViV_{i}, any color is used either zero times or at least δ​|Vi|\delta|V_{i}| times, we will still have |𝒞2|≥e−cδ​n​|𝒞1||\mathcal{C}_{2}|\geq e^{-c_{\delta}n}|\mathcal{C}_{1}|. Here, cδc_{\delta} is a constant which tends to zero with δ\delta. Now each coloring in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} has the special property that whenever the same color appears on two parts ViV_{i} and VjV_{j}, then there cannot be any edges between those entire parts.

Claim 3.

By looking at which colors appear on each part ViV_{i}, we may associate each coloring with a map from [M]→2[q][M]\rightarrow 2^{[q]}. Let ϕ:[M]→2[q]\phi:[M]\rightarrow 2^{[q]} be a map which is associated with the maximum number of colorings in 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}. Then, if we keep only those colorings 𝒞3⊂𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{3}\subset\mathcal{C}_{2} which give ϕ\phi, we still have |𝒞3|≥2−q​M​|𝒞2||\mathcal{C}_{3}|\geq 2^{-qM}|\mathcal{C}_{2}|.

Claim 4.

For every A⊂[q]A\subset[q], let VAV_{A} be the union of those parts ViV_{i} for which ϕ⁡(i)=A\phi(i)=A. (These are the parts that in all colorings in 𝒞3\mathcal{C}_{3} are colored using exactly colors from AA.) Define the vector 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} by setting each αA=|VA|/n\alpha_{A}=|V_{A}|/n. Then G′⊂G𝜶​(n)G^{\prime}\subset G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n), and since G′G^{\prime} only differs from our original GG by at most δ​n2\delta n^{2} edges, we also have 𝜶∈Feas​(m/n2−δ){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\text{\sc Feas}(m/n^{2}-\delta). Thus:

|𝒞3|≤∏A⊂[q]|A||VA|=eobj​(𝜶)​n≤eopt​(m/n2−δ)​n.|\mathcal{C}_{3}|\ \leq\ \prod_{A\subset[q]}|A|^{|V_{A}|}\ =\ e^{\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})n}\ \leq\ e^{\text{\sc opt}(m/n^{2}-\delta)n}\,.
Claim 5.

The function opt is uniformly continuous. Thus, for an appropriate (sufficiently small) choice of δ>0\delta>0, we have for all sufficiently large nn that

PG​(q)≤PG′​(q)≤ecδ​n⋅2q​M⋅eopt​(m/n2−δ)​n<e(opt​(m/n2)+ϵ)​n,P_{G}(q)\ \leq\ P_{G^{\prime}}(q)\ \leq\ e^{c_{\delta}n}\cdot 2^{qM}\cdot e^{\text{\sc opt}(m/n^{2}-\delta)n}\ <\ e^{(\text{\sc opt}(m/n^{2})+\epsilon)n}\,,

as desired. (Recall that PG​(q)P_{G}(q) is the number of qq-colorings of GG.)

By combining these five claims with an elementary analysis argument, we also obtain a stability result, which roughly states that if a graph has “close” to the optimal number of colorings, then it must resemble a graph from Construction 1. A stability result is very useful, because the approximate structure later allows us to apply combinatorial arguments to refine our asymptotic results into exact results. We quantify this in terms of the edit-distance, which we defined in Section 2. Recall that we say two graphs are dd-close when their edit distance is at most dd. We prove the following theorem in Section 3.5.

Theorem 3.3.

For any ϵ,κ>0\epsilon,\kappa>0, the following holds for all sufficiently large nn. Let GG be an nn-vertex, graph with m≤κ​n2m\leq\kappa n^{2} edges, which maximizes the number of qq-colorings. Then GG is ϵ​n2\epsilon n^{2}-close to some G𝛂​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n) from Construction 1, for an 𝛂{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} which solves opt​(γ)\text{\sc opt}(\gamma) for some |γ−m/n2|≤ϵ|\gamma-m/n^{2}|\leq\epsilon with γ≤κ\gamma\leq\kappa.

Remark.  This theorem is only useful if the resulting γ\gamma falls within the range of densities for which the solution of opt is known. The technical parameter κ\kappa is used to keep γ\gamma within this range.

3.2 Finer resolution in the sparse case

The Regularity Lemma is nontrivial only for graphs with positive edge density (i.e., quadratic number of edges). This typically presents a serious and often insurmountable obstacle when trying to extend Regularity-based results to situations involving sparse graphs. Although much work has been done to develop sparse variants of the Regularity Lemma, the resulting analogues are weaker and much more difficult to apply.

Let us illustrate the issue by attempting to apply Theorem 3.2 when m=o⁡(n2)m=o(n^{2}). Then, we find that the maximum number of qq-colorings of any nn-vertex graph with mm edges is ec​n+o⁡(n)e^{cn+o(n)}, where c=opt​(0)c=\text{\sc opt}(0) is a constant entirely determined by qq. Note that the final asymptotic is independent of mm, even if mm grows extremely slowly compared to n2n^{2}. This is because the key parameter was the density m/n2m/n^{2}, which already vanished once m=o⁡(n2)m=o(n^{2}). Thus, the interesting question in the sparse case is to distinguish between sparse graphs and very sparse graphs, by looking inside the o⁡(n)o(n) error term in the exponent.

We are able to circumvent these difficulties by making the following key observation which allows us to pass to a dense subgraph. As it turns out, every sparse graph which maximizes the number of qq-colorings has a nice structure: most of the vertices are isolated, and all of the edges are contained in a subgraph which is dense, but not too dense. Section 3.6 contains the following lemma’s short proof, which basically boils down to a comparison against the smallest Turán graph with at least mm edges.

Lemma 3.4.

Fix an integer q≥2q\geq 2 and a threshold κ>0\kappa>0. Given any positive integer mm, there exists an n0=Θ⁡(m)n_{0}=\Theta(\sqrt{m}) with m/n02≤κm/n_{0}^{2}\leq\kappa such that the following holds for any n≥n0n\geq n_{0}. In every nn-vertex graph GG with mm edges, which maximizes the number of qq-colorings, there is a set of n0n_{0} vertices which spans all of the edges.

The fact that our graph is sparse becomes a benefit rather than a drawback, because it allows us to limit the edge density from above by any fixed threshold. This is useful, because it turns out that we can completely solve the optimization problem for all densities below κq=(log⁡q/(q−1)log⁡q+log⁡qlog⁡q/(q−1))−2\kappa_{q}=\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log q/(q-1)}{\log q}}+\sqrt{\frac{\log q}{\log q/(q-1)}}\right)^{-2}. We will prove the following proposition in Section 4.1.

Proposition 3.5.

Fix an integer q≥3q\geq 3. For any 0≤γ≤κq0\leq\gamma\leq\kappa_{q}, the unique solution (up to a permutation of the ground set [q][q]) to opt​(γ)\text{\sc opt}(\gamma) has the following form.

α{1}=γ⋅log⁡qq−1/log⁡q,α{2,…​q}=γα{1},α[q]=1−α{1}−α{2,…​q},\alpha_{\{1\}}=\sqrt{\gamma\cdot\log\frac{q}{q-1}\,/\,\log q},\quad\quad\alpha_{\{2,\ldots q\}}=\frac{\gamma}{\alpha_{\{1\}}},\quad\quad\alpha_{[q]}=1-\alpha_{\{1\}}-\alpha_{\{2,\ldots q\}}, (1)

with all other αA=0\alpha_{A}=0. This gives opt​(γ)=log⁡q−2​γ⋅log⁡qq−1⋅log⁡q\text{\sc opt}(\gamma)=\log q-2\sqrt{\gamma\cdot\log\frac{q}{q-1}\cdot\log q}.

Since we have the complete solution of the relevant instance of the optimization problem, we can give explicit bounds when we transfer our asymptotic results from the previous section to the sparse case. We can also explicitly describe the graph that approximates any optimal graph, as follows. Let t1t_{1} and t2t_{2} be real numbers that satisfy t1/t2=log⁡qq−1/log⁡qt_{1}/t_{2}=\log\frac{q}{q-1}/\log q and t1​t2=mt_{1}t_{2}=m. Take a complete bipartite graph between two vertex clusters V1V_{1} and V2V_{2} with sizes |Vi|=⌈ti⌉|V_{i}|=\lceil t_{i}\rceil, and add enough isolated vertices to make the total number of vertices exactly nn. Call the result Gn,mG_{n,m}.

Proposition 3.6.

Fix an integer q≥3q\geq 3. The following hold for all sufficiently large m≤κq​n2m\leq\kappa_{q}n^{2}.

(i)

The maximum number of qq-colorings of an nn-vertex graph with mm edges is qn​e(c+o⁡(1))​mq^{n}e^{(c+o(1))\sqrt{m}}, where c=−2​log⁡qq−1​log⁡qc=-2\sqrt{\log\frac{q}{q-1}\log q}. Here, the o⁡(1)o(1) term tends to zero as m→∞m\rightarrow\infty.

(ii)

For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, as long as mm is sufficiently large, every nn-vertex graph GG with mm edges, which maximizes the number of qq-colorings, is ϵ​m\epsilon m-close to the graph Gn,mG_{n,m} which we described above.

We prove this proposition in Section 3.6. Note that part (i) is precisely the final claim of Theorem 1.2.

This section contains the proofs of the claims in Section 3.1, except for Claim 3, which is obvious. Together, these establish part (i) of Theorem 3.2, which gives the asymptotic upper bound for the number of qq-colorings of an nn-vertex graph with mm edges.

Proof of Claim 1.  Apply Szemerédi’s Regularity Lemma (Theorem 2.2) with parameter ϵ=δ/3\epsilon=\delta/3 to partition of VV into nearly-equal parts V1V_{1}, …, VMV_{M}. (1+o⁡(1))​[M​(n/M2)+ϵ​M2​(n/M)2+ϵ​(n2)]≤(1+o⁡(1))​[ϵ​n2/2+ϵ​n2+ϵ​n2/2],(1+o(1))\left[M{n/M\choose 2}+\epsilon M^{2}(n/M)^{2}+\epsilon{n\choose 2}\right]\ \leq\ (1+o(1))[\epsilon n^{2}/2+\epsilon n^{2}+\epsilon n^{2}/2],

which is indeed less than δ​n2\delta n^{2} when nn is sufficiently large.

It remains to show property (ii). The only edges remaining in G′G^{\prime} are those between ϵ\epsilon-regular pairs (Vi,Vj)(V_{i},V_{j}) with edge-density greater than ϵ\epsilon. By definition of ϵ\epsilon-regularity (and since OPENδ>ϵ)\delta>\epsilon), the edge density between every pair of sets |U|≥δ​|Vi||U|\geq\delta|V_{i}|, |W|≥δ​|Vj||W|\geq\delta|V_{j}| must be positive. In particular, there must be at least one edge, which establishes property (ii). □\Box

Proof of Claim 2.  We show that |𝒞2|≥e−cδ​n​|𝒞1||\mathcal{C}_{2}|\geq e^{-c_{\delta}n}|\mathcal{C}_{1}|, with cδ=q​δ​log⁡e2δc_{\delta}=q\delta\log\frac{e^{2}}{\delta}. 3.4 Proof of Theorem 3.2, part (ii)

In this section, we establish the asymptotic tightness of our upper bound, by showing that Construction 2 produces graphs that asymptotically maximize the number of qq-colorings. We will need Proposition 3.1, so we prove it first.

Proof of Proposition 3.1.  Define the variables nA=n​αAn_{A}=n\alpha_{A} (not necessarily integers), and call the expressions ∑AnA\sum_{A}n_{A} and ∑A∩B=∅nA​nB\sum_{A\cap B=\emptyset}n_{A}n_{B} the numbers of fractional vertices and fractional edges, respectively. Initially, there are exactly nn fractional vertices and e​(𝜶)​n2\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})n^{2} fractional edges.

Recall that the construction rounds each nAn_{A} either up or down to the next integer. Let us perform these individual roundings sequentially, finishing all of the downward roundings before the upward roundings. This ensures that the number of fractional vertices is kept ≤n\leq n throughout the process. But each iteration changes the number of fractional edges by at most ∑AnA≤n\sum_{A}n_{A}\leq n, and there are at most 2q2^{q} iterations, so our final number of edges is indeed within 2q​n2^{q}n of mm.

The second part of the proposition is proved similarly. We can apply the same iterative process to change each part size from αA​n\alpha_{A}n to νA​n\nu_{A}n, in such a way that all downward adjustments are performed first. When updating the coordinate indexed by A⊂[q]A\subset[q], we affect at most (|αA​n−νA​n|+2)​n(|\alpha_{A}n-\nu_{A}n|+2)n edges, where the extra 2 comes from the fact that the part sizes were rounded off. Therefore, after the ≤2q\leq 2^{q} total iterations, the total number of edges we edit is indeed at most ‖𝜶−𝝂‖1​n2+2q+1​n\|{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\|_{1}n^{2}+2^{q+1}n. □\Box

Proof of Theorem 3.2(ii).  Let nn and mm be given, with mm less than the number of edges in the Turán graph Tq​(n)T_{q}(n). Suppose we have a vector 𝜶∈Feas​(m/n2){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\text{\sc Feas}(m/n^{2}) which achieves the maximum obj​(𝜶)=opt​(m/n2)\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\text{\sc opt}(m/n^{2}). Construction 2 produces a graph G𝜶′​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\prime}(n) with nn vertices and at least mm edges, which we will show has more than e(opt​(m/n2)−ϵ)​ne^{(\text{\sc opt}(m/n^{2})-\epsilon)n} proper qq-colorings, as long as nn is sufficiently large.

If G𝜶​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n) already has at least mm edges, then we defined G𝜶′​(n)=G𝜶​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\prime}(n)=G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n), which has at least ∏A|A|⌊n​αA⌋≥∏A|A|n​αA−1=eobj​(𝜶)​n/∏A|A|=eobj​(𝜶)​n−O​(1)\prod_{A}|A|^{\lfloor n\alpha_{A}\rfloor}\geq\prod_{A}|A|^{n\alpha_{A}-1}=e^{\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})n}/\prod_{A}|A|=e^{\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})n-O(1)} colorings, because all colorings that use only colors from AA for each VAV_{A} are proper.

Otherwise, G𝜶​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n) is short by, say, kk edges, which is ≤2q​n\leq 2^{q}n by Proposition 3.1. If the largest |VA||V_{A}| indexed by a non-singleton is at least 2​⌈k⌉2\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil, our construction places a kk-edge bipartite graph between U1,U2⊂VAU_{1},U_{2}\subset V_{A}. Let c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} be two distinct colors in AA. Even if we force every vertex in each UiU_{i} to take the color cic_{i}, we only lose at most a factor of q2​⌈k⌉=eo⁡(n)q^{2\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil}=e^{o(n)} compared to the bound in the previous paragraph. This is because each of the 2​⌈k⌉2\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil vertices in U1∪U2U_{1}\cup U_{2} had its number of color choices reduced from |A|≤q|A|\leq q to 1. So, G𝜶′​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\prime}(n) still has at least eobj​(𝜶)​n−o​(n)e^{\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})n-o(n)} colorings.

The final case is when all parts VAV_{A} indexed by non-singletons are smaller than 2​⌈k⌉2\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil. Here, the construction simply defines G𝜶′​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\prime}(n) to be the Turán graph Tq​(n)T_{q}(n). Since log⁡|A|=0\log|A|=0 for singletons AA, the upper bound on |VA||V_{A}| implies that obj​(𝜶)≤2q⋅2​⌈k⌉n⋅log⁡q\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq 2^{q}\cdot\frac{2\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil}{n}\cdot\log q. This is less than ϵ\epsilon for sufficiently large nn, because we had k≤2q​nk\leq 2^{q}n. Then, e(opt​(m/n2)−ϵ)​n<1e^{(\text{\sc opt}(m/n^{2})-\epsilon)n}<1, which is of course less than the number of qq-colorings of the Turán graph Tq​(n)T_{q}(n). This completes our proof. □\Box

3.5 Proof of Theorem 3.3

In this section, we prove that any nn-vertex graph with mm edges, which maximizes the number of qq-colorings, is in fact close (in edit-distance) to a graph G𝜶​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n) from Construction 1. In fact, we prove something slightly stronger: if a graph has “close” to the maximum number of qq-colorings, then it must be “close” (in edit-distance) to an asymptotically optimal graph from Construction 1.

Lemma 3.7.

For any ϵ,κ>0\epsilon,\kappa>0, there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that the following holds for all sufficiently large nn. Let GG be an nn-vertex graph with m≤κ​n2m\leq\kappa n^{2} edges and at least e(opt​(m/n2)−δ)​ne^{(\text{\sc opt}(m/n^{2})-\delta)n} proper qq-colorings. Then GG is ϵ​n2\epsilon n^{2}-close to some G𝛂​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n) from Construction 1, for an 𝛂{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} which solves opt​(γ)\text{\sc opt}(\gamma) for some |γ−m/n2|≤ϵ|\gamma-m/n^{2}|\leq\epsilon with γ≤κ\gamma\leq\kappa.

Note that this lemma immediately implies Theorem 3.3, because Theorem 3.2 established that the maximum number of colorings of an nn-vertex graph with mm edges was e(opt​(m/n2)+o⁡(1))​ne^{(\text{\sc opt}(m/n^{2})+o(1))n}. Its proof is an elementary analysis exercise in compactness, which only requires the continuity of obj, opt, v, and e, the fact that 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} and the edge densities m/n2m/n^{2} reside in compact spaces, and the following consequence of Claims 1–4 of Section 3.1 (whose simple proof we omit):

Corollary 3.8.

For every δ>0\delta>0, the following holds for all sufficiently large nn. Every qq-colorable, nn-vertex graph GG with mm edges is δ​n2\delta n^{2}-close to a subgraph of some G𝛂​(n)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n) with 𝛂∈Feas​(m/n2−δ){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\text{\sc Feas}(m/n^{2}-\delta). Also, GG has at most e(obj​(𝛂)+δ)​ne^{(\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\delta)n} proper qq-colorings.

Proof of Lemma 3.7.  We proceed by contradiction. Then, there is some fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0, a sequence δi→0\delta_{i}\rightarrow 0, and a sequence of graphs GiG_{i} with the following properties.

(i)

GiG_{i} has at least as many vertices as required to apply Corollary 3.8 with parameter δi\delta_{i}.

(ii)

GiG_{i} has at least e(opt​(mi/ni2)−δi)​nie^{(\text{\sc opt}(m_{i}/n_{i}^{2})-\delta_{i})n_{i}} colorings, where nin_{i} and mim_{i} are its numbers of vertices and edges, and mi≤κ​ni2m_{i}\leq\kappa n_{i}^{2}.

(iii)

GiG_{i} is at least ϵ​ni2\epsilon n_{i}^{2}-far from G𝜶​(ni)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n_{i}) for every 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} that solves opt​(γ)\text{\sc opt}(\gamma) with |γ−mi/ni2|≤ϵ|\gamma-m_{i}/n_{i}^{2}|\leq\epsilon.

Applying Corollary 3.8 to each GiG_{i} with parameter δi\delta_{i}, we find that there are vectors 𝜶i∈Feas​(mi/ni2−δi){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}\in\text{\sc Feas}(m_{i}/n_{i}^{2}-\delta_{i}) such that GiG_{i} is δi​ni2\delta_{i}n_{i}^{2}-close to some subgraph Gi′G_{i}^{\prime} of G𝜶i​(ni)G_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}}(n_{i}), and each GiG_{i} has at most e(obj​(𝜶i)+δi)​nie^{(\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i})+\delta_{i})n_{i}} proper qq-colorings. Combining this with property (ii) above, we find that each obj​(𝜶i)≥opt​(mi/ni2)−2​δi\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i})\geq\text{\sc opt}(m_{i}/n_{i}^{2})-2\delta_{i}. The densities mi/ni2m_{i}/n_{i}^{2} and the vectors 𝜶i{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i} live in bounded (hence compact) spaces. So, by passing to a subsequence, we may assume that mi/ni2→γ≤κm_{i}/n_{i}^{2}\rightarrow\gamma\leq\kappa and 𝜶i→𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}\rightarrow{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} for some limit points γ\gamma and 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}.

Observe that by continuity, both 𝜶∈Feas​(γ){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\text{\sc Feas}(\gamma) and obj​(𝜶)≥opt​(γ)\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq\text{\sc opt}(\gamma). Therefore 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} solves opt​(γ)\text{\sc opt}(\gamma), i.e., obj​(𝜶)=opt​(γ)\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\text{\sc opt}(\gamma). Furthermore, although a priori we only knew that e​(𝜶)≥γ\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq\gamma, maximality implies that in fact e​(𝜶)=γ\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\gamma. Indeed, if not then one could shift more mass to α[q]\alpha_{[q]} to increase obj​(𝜶)\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) while staying within the feasible set. This would contradict that obj​(𝜶)=opt​(γ)\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\text{\sc opt}(\gamma).

We finish by showing that eventually GiG_{i} is ϵ​ni2\epsilon n_{i}^{2}-close to G𝜶​(ni)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n_{i}), contradicting (iii). To do this, we show that all three of the edit-distances between Gi↔Gi′↔G𝜶i​(ni)↔G𝜶​(ni)G_{i}\leftrightarrow G_{i}^{\prime}\leftrightarrow G_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}}(n_{i})\leftrightarrow G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n_{i}) are o⁡(ni2)o(n_{i}^{2}). The closeness of the first pair follows by construction since δi→0\delta_{i}\rightarrow 0, and the closeness of the last pair follows from Proposition 3.1 because 𝜶i→𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}\rightarrow{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}.

For the central pair, recall that Gi′G_{i}^{\prime} is actually contained in G𝜶i​(ni)G_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}}(n_{i}), so we only need to compare their numbers of edges. In fact, since we already established o⁡(ni2)o(n_{i}^{2})-closeness of the first and last pairs, it suffices to show that the difference between the number of edges in GiG_{i} and G𝜶​(ni)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n_{i}) is o⁡(ni2)o(n_{i}^{2}). Recall from above that e​(𝜶)=γ\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\gamma, and therefore by Proposition 3.1, G𝜶​(ni)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n_{i}) has e​(𝜶)​ni2+o⁡(ni2)=(γ+o⁡(1))​ni2\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})n_{i}^{2}+o(n_{i}^{2})=(\gamma+o(1))n_{i}^{2} edges. Yet GiG_{i} also has (γ+o⁡(1))​ni2(\gamma+o(1))n_{i}^{2} edges, because mi/ni2→γm_{i}/n_{i}^{2}\rightarrow\gamma. This completes the proof. □\Box

3.6 Proofs for the sparse case

In this section, we prove the statements which refine our results in the case when the graph is sparse, i.e., m=o⁡(n2)m=o(n^{2}). We begin with the lemma which shows that every sparse graph with the maximum number of colorings has a dense core which spans all of the edges.

Proof of Lemma 3.4.  Let n1n_{1} be the number of non-isolated vertices in GG, and let rr be the number of connected components in the subgraph induced by the non-isolated vertices. Since all such vertices there have degree at least 1, we have r≤n1/2r\leq n_{1}/2.

Any connected graph on tt vertices has at most q​(q−1)t−1q(q-1)^{t-1} proper qq-colorings, because we may iteratively color the vertices along a depth-first-search tree rooted at an arbitrary vertex; when we visit any vertex other than the root, there will only be at most q−1q-1 colors left to choose from. So, GG has at most qn−n1⋅qr⋅(q−1)n1−rq^{n-n_{1}}\cdot q^{r}\cdot(q-1)^{n_{1}-r} colorings, where the first factor comes from the fact that isolated vertices have a free choice over all qq colors. Using r≤n1/2r\leq n_{1}/2, this bound is at most qn−n1/2​(q−1)n1/2q^{n-n_{1}/2}(q-1)^{n_{1}/2}.

But since GG is optimal, it must have at least as many colorings as the Turán graph Tq​(n2)T_{q}(n_{2}) plus n−n2n-n_{2} isolated vertices, where n2=Θ⁡(m)n_{2}=\Theta(\sqrt{m}) is the minimum number of vertices in a qq-partite Turán graph with at least mm edges. The isolated vertices already give the latter graph at least qn−n2q^{n-n_{2}} colorings, so we must have qn−n2≤qn−n1/2​(q−1)n1/2q^{n-n_{2}}\leq q^{n-n_{1}/2}(q-1)^{n_{1}/2}, which implies that

n1≤n2⋅(2​log⁡q)/(log⁡qq−1).n_{1}\leq n_{2}\cdot(2\log q)/\left(\log\frac{q}{q-1}\right). (2)

The expression on the right hand side is Θ⁡(n2)=Θ⁡(m)\Theta(n_{2})=\Theta(\sqrt{m}), so if we define the integer n0n_{0} to be the maximum of right hand side in (2) and m/κ\sqrt{m/\kappa} (rounding up to the next integer if necessary) then we indeed have n1≤n0=Θ⁡(n2)=Θ⁡(m)n_{1}\leq n_{0}=\Theta(n_{2})=\Theta(\sqrt{m}). □\Box

Next, we prove the first part of Proposition 3.6, which claims that the maximum number of qq-colorings of an nn-vertex graph with m≤κq​n2m\leq\kappa_{q}n^{2} edges is asymptotically qn​e(c+o⁡(1))​mq^{n}e^{(c+o(1))\sqrt{m}}, where κq=(log⁡q/(q−1)log⁡q+log⁡qlog⁡q/(q−1))−2\kappa_{q}=\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log q/(q-1)}{\log q}}+\sqrt{\frac{\log q}{\log q/(q-1)}}\right)^{-2} and c=−2​log⁡qq−1​log⁡qc=-2\sqrt{\log\frac{q}{q-1}\log q}.

Proof of Proposition 3.6(i).  Let GG be an nn-vertex graph with mm edges, which maximizes the number of qq-colorings. Let n0n_{0} be the integer obtained by applying Lemma 3.4 with threshold κq\kappa_{q}. If n≥n0n\geq n_{0}, the lemma gives a dense n0n_{0}-vertex subgraph G′⊂GG^{\prime}\subset G which contains all of the edges. Otherwise, set G′=GG^{\prime}=G. In either case, we obtain a graph G′G^{\prime} whose number of vertices n′n^{\prime} is Θ⁡(m)\Theta(\sqrt{m}), and m/(n′)2≤κqm/(n^{\prime})^{2}\leq\kappa_{q}.

Since the vertices in G∖G′G\setminus G^{\prime} (if any) are isolated, the number of qq-colorings of GG is precisely qn−n′q^{n-n^{\prime}} times the number of qq-colorings of G′G^{\prime}. Therefore, G′G^{\prime} must also have the maximum number of qq-colorings over all n′n^{\prime}-vertex graphs with mm edges. Applying Theorem 3.2 to G′G^{\prime}, we find that G′G^{\prime} has e(opt​(m/(n′)2)+o⁡(1))​n′e^{(\text{\sc opt}(m/(n^{\prime})^{2})+o(1))n^{\prime}} colorings. Proposition 3.5 gives us the precise answer opt​(m/(n′)2)=log⁡q−2​m(n′)2⋅log⁡qq−1⋅log⁡q\text{\sc opt}(m/(n^{\prime})^{2})=\log q-2\sqrt{\frac{m}{(n^{\prime})^{2}}\cdot\log\frac{q}{q-1}\cdot\log q}, so substituting that in gives us that the number of qq-colorings of GG is:

qn−n′⋅e(opt​(m/(n′)2)+o⁡(1))​n′=qn−n′⋅qn′​e(c+o⁡(1))​m=qn​e(c+o⁡(1))​m,q^{n-n^{\prime}}\cdot e^{(\text{\sc opt}(m/(n^{\prime})^{2})+o(1))n^{\prime}}\ =\ q^{n-n^{\prime}}\cdot q^{n^{\prime}}e^{(c+o(1))\sqrt{m}}\ =\ q^{n}e^{(c+o(1))\sqrt{m}},

where cc is indeed the same constant as claimed in the statement of this proposition. □\Box

We finish this section by proving the stability result which shows that any optimal sparse graph is ϵ​m\epsilon m-close (in edit-distance) to the graph Gn,mG_{n,m} defined in Section 3.2.

Proof of Proposition 3.6(ii).  Let GG be an nn-vertex graph with mm edges, which maximizes the number of qq-colorings. We will actually show the equivalent statement that GG is O⁡((ϵ+ϵ)​m)O((\epsilon+\sqrt{\epsilon})m)-close to Gn,mG_{n,m}.

As in the proof of part (i) above, we find a dense n′n^{\prime}-vertex subgraph G′⊂GG^{\prime}\subset G that spans all of the edges, which itself must maximize the number of qq-colorings. Using the same parameters as above, we have n′=Θ⁡(m)n^{\prime}=\Theta(\sqrt{m}) and m≤κq​(n′)2m\leq\kappa_{q}(n^{\prime})^{2}. By Theorem 3.3, G′G^{\prime} must be ϵ​(n′)2\epsilon(n^{\prime})^{2}-close to a graph G𝜶​(n′)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n^{\prime}) from Construction 1, for some 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} that solves opt​(γ)\text{\sc opt}(\gamma) with γ≤κq\gamma\leq\kappa_{q}. Since n′=Θ⁡(m)n^{\prime}=\Theta(\sqrt{m}), the graphs are O⁡(ϵ​m)O(\epsilon m)-close. The γ\gamma is within the range in which Proposition 3.5 solved Optimization Problem 1, so G𝜶​(n′)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n^{\prime}) is a complete bipartite graph plus isolated vertices, which indeed resembles Gn,mG_{n,m}.

Moreover, the ratio between the sizes of the sides of the complete bipartite graph in G𝜶​(n′)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n^{\prime}) is correct, because it tends to the constant log⁡qq−1/log⁡q\log\frac{q}{q-1}/\log q regardless of the value of γ\gamma. Also, their product, which equals the number of edges in G𝜶​(n′)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n^{\prime}), is within O⁡(ϵ​m)O(\epsilon m) of mm because G𝜶​(n′)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n^{\prime}) is O⁡(ϵ​m)O(\epsilon m)-close to the mm-edge graph G′G^{\prime}. Therefore, each of the sides of the complete bipartite graph in G𝜶​(n′)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n^{\prime}) differs in size from its corresponding side in Gn,mG_{n,m} by at most O⁡(ϵ​m)O(\sqrt{\epsilon m}). Since each side of the bipartite graph in Gn,mG_{n,m} has size Θ⁡(m)\Theta(\sqrt{m}), we can transform G𝜶​(n′)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n^{\prime}) into Gn,mG_{n,m} by adding isolated vertices and editing at most O⁡(ϵ⋅m)O(\sqrt{\epsilon}\cdot m) edges. Yet by construction of 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}, the graphs G′G^{\prime} and G𝜶​(n′)G_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(n^{\prime}) were O⁡(ϵ​m)O(\epsilon m)-close, modulo isolated vertices. Therefore, GG and Gn,mG_{n,m} are indeed O⁡((ϵ+ϵ)​m)O((\epsilon+\sqrt{\epsilon})m)-close, as claimed. □\Box

4 Solving the optimization problem

In this section, we solve the optimization problem for low densities, for all values of qq. We also solve it for all densities in the case when q=3q=3.

4.1 Sparse case

The key observation is that when the edge density is low, we can reduce the optimization problem to one with no edge density parameter and no vertex constraint. This turns out to be substantially easier to solve.

Optimization Problem 2.  Fix an integer qq, and consider the following objective and constraint functions:

obj∗​(𝜶):=∑AαA​log⁡|A|q;e​(𝜶):=∑A∩B=∅αA​αB.\text{\sc obj}^{*}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}):=\sum_{A}\alpha_{A}\log\frac{|A|}{q}\,;\quad\quad\quad\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}):=\sum_{A\cap B=\emptyset}\alpha_{A}\alpha_{B}.

The vector 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} has 2q−22^{q}-2 coordinates αA∈ℝ\alpha_{A}\in\mathbb{R} indexed by the nonempty proper subsets A⊂[q]A\subset[q], and the sum in e​(𝜶)\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) runs over unordered pairs of disjoint sets {A,B}\{A,B\}. Let Feas∗\text{\sc Feas}^{*} be the feasible set of vectors defined by the constraints 𝜶≥0{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\geq 0 and e​(𝜶)≥1\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq 1. We seek to maximize obj∗​(𝜶)\text{\sc obj}^{*}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) over the set Feas∗\text{\sc Feas}^{*}, and we define opt∗\text{\sc opt}^{*} to be this maximum value, which we will show to exist in Section 4.1.1. We write that the vector 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} solves opt∗\text{\sc opt}^{*} when both 𝜶∈Feas∗{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\text{\sc Feas}^{*} and obj∗​(𝜶)=opt∗\text{\sc obj}^{*}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\text{\sc opt}^{*}.

Proposition 4.1.

For any given q≥3q\geq 3, the unique solution (up to a permutation of the base set [q][q]) to Optimization Problem 2 is the vector 𝛂∗{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*} with

α{1}∗=log⁡qq−1/log⁡q,α{2,…​q}∗=1α{1}∗,and all other αA∗=0.\alpha_{\{1\}}^{*}=\sqrt{\log\frac{q}{q-1}\,/\,\log q},\quad\quad\quad\alpha_{\{2,\ldots q\}}^{*}=\frac{1}{\alpha_{\{1\}}^{*}},\quad\quad\quad\text{and all other $\alpha_{A}^{*}=0$.}

This gives obj∗​(𝛂∗)=−2​log⁡qq−1​log⁡q\text{\sc obj}^{*}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})=-2\sqrt{\log\frac{q}{q-1}\log q}.

Let us show how Proposition 4.1 implies Proposition 3.5, which gave the solution to Optimization Problem 1 for sufficiently low edge densities γ\gamma.

Proof of Proposition 3.5.  Let 𝜶∗{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*} be the unique maximizer for Optimization Problem 2, and consider any number t≥v​(𝜶∗)t\geq\text{\sc v}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}). Then 𝜶∗{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*} is still the unique maximizer of obj∗​(𝜶)\text{\sc obj}^{*}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) when 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} is required to satisfy the vacuous condition v​(𝜶)≤t\text{\sc v}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq t as well. Let 𝜶¯\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}} be the vector obtained by dividing every entry of 𝜶∗{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*} by tt, and adding a new entry α¯[q]\overline{\alpha}_{[q]} so that v​(𝜶¯)=1\text{\sc v}(\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}})=1.

Then, 𝜶¯\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}} is the unique maximizer of obj∗​(𝜶)\text{\sc obj}^{*}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) when 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} is constrained by v​(𝜶)=1\text{\sc v}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=1 and e​(𝜶)≥t−2\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq t^{-2}. But when v​(𝜶)=1\text{\sc v}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=1 is one of the constraints, then obj∗​(𝜶)=obj​(𝜶)−log⁡q\text{\sc obj}^{*}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\log q, so this implies that 𝜶¯\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}} is the unique solution to opt​(t−2)\text{\sc opt}(t^{-2}). Using the substitution γ=t−2\gamma=t^{-2}, we see that 𝜶¯\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}} is precisely the vector described in (1). Since t≥v​(𝜶∗)t\geq\text{\sc v}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}) was arbitrary, we conclude that this holds for all γ\gamma below v​(𝜶∗)−2=(log⁡q/(q−1)log⁡q+log⁡qlog⁡q/(q−1))−2=κq\text{\sc v}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})^{-2}=\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log q/(q-1)}{\log q}}+\sqrt{\frac{\log q}{\log q/(q-1)}}\right)^{-2}=\kappa_{q}. □\Box

4.1.1 Observations for Optimization Problem 2

We begin by showing that obj∗\text{\sc obj}^{*} attains its maximum on the feasible set Feas∗\text{\sc Feas}^{*}. Since Feas∗\text{\sc Feas}^{*} is clearly nonempty, there is some finite c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} for which opt∗≥c\text{\sc opt}^{*}\geq c. In the formula for obj∗\text{\sc obj}^{*}, all coefficients log⁡|A|q\log\frac{|A|}{q} of the αA\alpha_{A} are negative, so we only need to consider the compact region bounded by 0≤αA≤c/log⁡|A|q0\leq\alpha_{A}\leq c/\log\frac{|A|}{q} for each AA. Therefore, by compactness, obj∗\text{\sc obj}^{*} indeed attains its maximum on Feas∗\text{\sc Feas}^{*}.

Now that we know the maximum is attained, we can use perturbation arguments to determine its location. The following definition will be convenient for our analysis.

Definition 4.2.

Let the support of a vector 𝛂{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} be the collection of AA for which αA≠0\alpha_{A}\neq 0.

The following lemma will allow us to reduce to the case of considering optimal vectors whose supports are a partition of [q][q].

Lemma 4.3.

One of the vectors 𝛂{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} which solves opt∗\text{\sc opt}^{*} has support that is a partition33 3 A collection of disjoint sets whose union is [q][q]. of [q][q]. Furthermore, if the only partitions that support optimal vectors consist of a singleton plus a (q−1)(q-1)-set, then in fact every vector which solves opt∗\text{\sc opt}^{*} is supported by such a partition.

Proof.  We begin with the first statement. Let 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} be a vector which solves opt∗\text{\sc opt}^{*}, and suppose that its support contains two intersecting sets AA and BB. We will perturb αA\alpha_{A} and αB\alpha_{B} while keeping all other α\alpha’s fixed. Since AA and BB intersect, the polynomial e​(𝜶)\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) has no products αA​αB\alpha_{A}\alpha_{B}, i.e., it is of the form x​αA+y​αB+zx\alpha_{A}+y\alpha_{B}+z, for some constants x,y,z≥0x,y,z\geq 0.

Furthermore, x≠0x\neq 0, or else we could reduce αA\alpha_{A} to zero without affecting e​(𝜶)\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}), but this would strictly increase obj∗​(𝜶)\text{\sc obj}^{*}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) because all coefficients log⁡|A|q\log\frac{|A|}{q} in obj∗\text{\sc obj}^{*} are negative. Similarly, y≠0y\neq 0. Therefore, we may perturb αA\alpha_{A} by +t​y+ty and αB\alpha_{B} by −t​x-tx, while keeping e​(𝜶)\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) fixed. Since we may use both positive and negative tt and obj∗\text{\sc obj}^{*} itself is linear in αA\alpha_{A} and αB\alpha_{B}, optimality implies that obj∗\text{\sc obj}^{*} does not depend on tt. Hence we may choose a tt which drives one of αA\alpha_{A} or αB\alpha_{B} to zero, and obj∗\text{\sc obj}^{*} will remain unchanged.

Repeating this process, we eventually obtain a vector 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} which is supported by disjoint sets. Their union must be the entire [q][q], because otherwise we could simply grow one of the sets in the support by adding the unused elements of [q][q]. This would not affect e​(𝜶)\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}), but it would strictly increase obj∗\text{\sc obj}^{*}.

It remains to prove the second part of our lemma. Let 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} be an optimal vector, and apply the above reduction process to simplify its support. At the end, we will have a vector supported by |A|=1|A|=1 and |B|=q−1|B|=q-1, by assumption. Each iteration of the reduction removes exactly one set from the support, so the second to last stage will have some 𝜶′{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\prime} supported by three distinct sets, two of which are the final AA and BB, and the third which we call CC.

In the reduction, when we consider two overlapping sets, we are free to select which one is removed. Therefore, we could choose to keep the third set CC and remove one of AA and BB, and then continue reducing until the support is disjoint, while keeping obj∗\text{\sc obj}^{*} unchanged. Yet no matter what CC was, it is impossible for this alternative reduction route to terminate in a partition of [q][q], contradicting the above observation that any reduction must terminate in a partition. □\Box

Definition 4.4.

Let 𝛂{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} be a fixed vector whose support is a partition of [q][q]. For each A⊂[q]A\subset[q], define the expressions:

IA=αA​∑B≠AαBJA=1obj∗​(𝜶)⋅αA​log⁡|A|q.I_{A}\ =\ \alpha_{A}\sum_{B\neq A}\alpha_{B}\quad\quad\quad J_{A}\ =\ \frac{1}{\text{\sc obj}^{*}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}\cdot\alpha_{A}\log\frac{|A|}{q}.
Lemma 4.5.

Let 𝛂{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} be a vector which solves opt∗\text{\sc opt}^{*}, whose support is a partition of [q][q]. Then:

(i)

For every A⊂[q]A\subset[q], we have IA=2​JAI_{A}=2J_{A}.

(ii)

In particular, for each AA in the support, IA/αA=2​JA/αAI_{A}/\alpha_{A}=2J_{A}/\alpha_{A}.

(iii)

Suppose AA and BB are both in the support, and |A|=|B||A|=|B|. Then αA=αB\alpha_{A}=\alpha_{B} as well.

Proof.  We begin with part (i). Fix any A⊂[q]A\subset[q]. Consider the following operation for small ϵ>0\epsilon>0. First, replace αA\alpha_{A} by (1+ϵ)​αA(1+\epsilon)\alpha_{A}. Observe that IA=αA∑B:B∩A=∅αBI_{A}=\alpha_{A}\sum_{B:B\cap A=\emptyset}\alpha_{B} because the support of 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} is a partition of [q][q]. Therefore we increase e​(𝜶)=∑A∩B=∅αA​αB\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\sum_{A\cap B=\emptyset}\alpha_{A}\alpha_{B} by ϵ​IA\epsilon I_{A}. Next, multiply all α\alpha’s (including the one we just increased) by (1+ϵIA)−1/2(1+\epsilon I_{A})^{-1/2}. Then e​(𝜶)\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) is still at least 1 and our perturbed vector is in Feas∗\text{\sc Feas}^{*}. Its new objective equals obj∗​(𝜶)⋅1+ϵ​JA1+ϵ​IA\text{\sc obj}^{*}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\cdot\frac{1+\epsilon J_{A}}{\sqrt{1+\epsilon I_{A}}}. Since 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} maximized the objective (which is always negative), we must have 1+ϵ​JA1+ϵ​IA≥1\frac{1+\epsilon J_{A}}{\sqrt{1+\epsilon I_{A}}}\geq 1. Rearranging, this implies that IA≤2​JA+ϵ​JA2I_{A}\leq 2J_{A}+\epsilon J_{A}^{2}. Sending ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0, we see that IA≤2​JAI_{A}\leq 2J_{A}. The opposite inequality follows from considering the replacement of αA\alpha_{A} by (1−ϵ)​αA(1-\epsilon)\alpha_{A}, and then multiplying α\alpha’s by (1−ϵIA)−1/2(1-\epsilon I_{A})^{-1/2}. This establishes part (i).

Part (ii) is obvious because αA≠0\alpha_{A}\neq 0 for AA in the support.

For part (iii), let S=∑CαCS=\sum_{C}\alpha_{C}. Since the support of 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} is a partition of [q][q], S−αA=IA/αAS-\alpha_{A}=I_{A}/\alpha_{A}. By part (ii), this equals 2​JA/αA=log⁡|A|q/obj∗​(𝜶)2J_{A}/\alpha_{A}=\log\frac{|A|}{q}/\text{\sc obj}^{*}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}), which is determined by the cardinality of AA. Therefore, S−αA=S−αBS-\alpha_{A}=S-\alpha_{B}, which implies (iii). □\Box

4.1.2 Solution to Optimization Problem 2 for 𝒒<𝟗\boldsymbol{q<9}

In its original form, Optimization Problem 2 involves exponentially many variables, but Lemma 4.3 dramatically reduces their number by allowing us to consider only supports that are partitions of [q][q]. Therefore, we need to make one computation per partition of [q][q], which can actually be done symbolically (hence exactly) by Mathematica. The running time of Mathematica’s symbolic maximization is double-exponential in the number of variables, so it was particularly helpful to reduce the number of variables.44 4 The entire computation for q∈{3,…,8}q\in\{3,\ldots,8\} took less than an hour. The complete Mathematica program and output accompany the arXiv version of this paper.

Let us illustrate this process by showing what needs to be done for the partition 7=2+2+37=2+2+3. This corresponds to maximizing αA​log⁡27+αB​log⁡27+αC​log⁡37\alpha_{A}\log\frac{2}{7}+\alpha_{B}\log\frac{2}{7}+\alpha_{C}\log\frac{3}{7} subject to the constraints αA​αB+αB​αC+αC​αA≥1\alpha_{A}\alpha_{B}+\alpha_{B}\alpha_{C}+\alpha_{C}\alpha_{A}\geq 1 and 𝜶≥0{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\geq 0. By Lemma 4.5(iii), we may assume αA=αB\alpha_{A}=\alpha_{B}, so it suffices to maximize 2​x​log⁡27+y​log⁡372x\log\frac{2}{7}+y\log\frac{3}{7} subject to x2+2​x​y≥1x^{2}+2xy\geq 1 and x,y≥0x,y\geq 0. This is achieved by Mathematica’s Maximize function:

Maximize[{2 x Log[2/7] + y Log[3/7], x^2 + 2 x y >= 1 && x >= 0 && y >= 0}, {x, y}]

Mathematica answers that the maximum value is −−(log⁡73)2+4​log⁡73​log​72≈−1.9-\sqrt{-\big(\log\frac{7}{3}\big)^{2}+4\log\frac{7}{3}\log\frac{7}{2}}\approx-1.9, which is indeed less than the claimed value −2​log⁡77−1​log⁡7≈−1.1-2\sqrt{\log\frac{7}{7-1}\log 7}\approx-1.1.

We performed one such computation per partition of each q∈{3,…,8}q\in\{3,\ldots,8\}. In every case except for the partition q=1+(q−1)q=1+(q-1), the maximum indeed fell short of the claimed value. That final partition is completely solved analytically (i.e., including the uniqueness result) by Lemma 4.6 in the next section. This completes the analysis for all q<9q<9.

4.1.3 Solution to Optimization Problem 2 for 𝒒≥𝟗\boldsymbol{q\geq 9}

We begin by ruling out several extreme partitions that our general argument below will not handle. As one may expect, each of these special cases has a fairly pedestrian proof, so we postpone the proofs of the following two lemmas to the appendix.

Lemma 4.6.

Fix any integer q≥3q\geq 3, and let 𝛂{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} be a vector which solves opt∗\text{\sc opt}^{*}. If the support of 𝛂{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} is a partition of [q][q] into exactly two sets, then (up to permutation of the ground set [q][q]) 𝛂{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} must be equal to the claimed unique optimal vector 𝛂∗{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*} in Proposition 4.1.

Lemma 4.7.

Fix any integer q≥4q\geq 4, and let 𝛂{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} be a vector which solves opt∗\text{\sc opt}^{*}, whose support is a partition of [q][q]. Then that partition cannot have any of the following forms:

(i)

all singletons;

(ii)

all singletons, except for one 2-set;

(iii)

have a (q−2)(q-2)-set as one of the parts.

The heart of the solution to the optimization problem is the following general case, which we will prove momentarily.

Lemma 4.8.

Fix any integer q≥9q\geq 9, and let 𝛂{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} be a vector which solves opt∗\text{\sc opt}^{*}, whose support is a partition of [q][q]. Then that partition must have a set of size at least q−2q-2.

These collected results show that opt∗\text{\sc opt}^{*} has the unique solution that we claimed at the beginning of this section.

Proof of Proposition 4.1 for q≥𝟗\boldsymbol{q\geq 9}.  Let 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} be a vector which solves opt∗\text{\sc opt}^{*}. By Lemma 4.3, we may assume that its support is a partition of [q][q]. It cannot be a single set (of cardinality qq), because then e​(𝜶)=0\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=0, and by Lemmas 4.7(iii) and 4.8, the support cannot contain a set of size ≤q−2\leq q-2.

Thus, the support must contain a set of size q−1q-1, and since it is a partition, the only other set is a singleton. Then Lemma 4.6 gives us that 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} equals the claimed unique optimal vector 𝜶∗{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}, up to a permutation of the ground set [q][q]. This completes the proof. □\Box

In the remainder of this section, we prove the general case (Lemma 4.8). The following definition and fact are convenient, but the proof is a routine calculus exercise, so we postpone it to the appendix.

4.2 Solving the optimization problem for 3 colors

In this section, we provide the complete analytic solution to Optimization Problem 1, for the entire range of the edge density parameter γ\gamma when the number of colors qq is exactly 3. To simplify notation, we will write α12\alpha_{12} instead of α{1,2}\alpha_{\{1,2\}}, etc.

Proposition 4.10.

Define the constant c=(log⁡3/2log⁡3+log⁡3log⁡3/2)−2≈0.1969c=\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log 3/2}{\log 3}}+\sqrt{\frac{\log 3}{\log 3/2}}\right)^{-2}\approx 0.1969. Then, the unique solution (up to a permutation of the index set {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\}) of Optimization Problem 1 with edge density parameter γ\gamma is the vector 𝛂{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} defined as follows. (All unspecified αA\alpha_{A} below are zero.)

(i)

If 0≤γ≤c0\leq\gamma\leq c, then α3=γ⋅log⁡3/2log⁡3\alpha_{3}=\sqrt{\gamma\cdot\frac{\log 3/2}{\log 3}}, α12=γα3\alpha_{12}=\frac{\gamma}{\alpha_{3}}, and α123=1−α12−α3\alpha_{123}=1-\alpha_{12}-\alpha_{3}. This gives opt​(γ)=log⁡3−2​γ⋅log⁡3⋅log⁡32\text{\sc opt}(\gamma)=\log 3-2\sqrt{\gamma\cdot\log 3\cdot\log\frac{3}{2}}.

(ii)

If c≤γ≤14c\leq\gamma\leq\frac{1}{4}, then α12=1+1−4​γ2\alpha_{12}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1-4\gamma}}{2} and α3=1−α12\alpha_{3}=1-\alpha_{12}, which gives opt​(γ)=1+1−4​γ2⋅log⁡2\text{\sc opt}(\gamma)=\frac{1+\sqrt{1-4\gamma}}{2}\cdot\log 2.

(iii)

If 14≤γ≤13\frac{1}{4}\leq\gamma\leq\frac{1}{3}, then α12=1−12​γ−32\alpha_{12}=\frac{1-\sqrt{12\gamma-3}}{2}, α1=α2=1−2​α123\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=\frac{1-2\alpha_{12}}{3}, and α3=1+α123\alpha_{3}=\frac{1+\alpha_{12}}{3}, which gives opt​(γ)=1−12​γ−32⋅log⁡2\text{\sc opt}(\gamma)=\frac{1-\sqrt{12\gamma-3}}{2}\cdot\log 2.

This covers the entire range of admissible γ\gamma, because γ=1/3\gamma=1/3 corresponds to the density of the Turán graph T3​(n)T_{3}(n), which is the densest 3-colorable graph.

4.2.1 Outline of solution

The strategy of the solution is as follows. Suppose we have some 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} that solves opt​(γ)\text{\sc opt}(\gamma). Since we may permute the index set, we may assume without loss of generality that α1≤α2≤α3\alpha_{1}\leq\alpha_{2}\leq\alpha_{3}. We then use perturbation arguments to pinpoint the location of 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}. Although the problem initially looks cumbersome (there are 7 nontrivially-related variables), the solution cleanly follows from 6 short steps.

Step 1.

By shifting mass55 5 Adjusting the values of the αA\alpha_{A} while conserving their sum ∑AαA=v​(𝜶)\sum_{A}\alpha_{A}=\text{\sc v}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}). between the αA\alpha_{A} with |A|=2|A|=2, we deduce that α23\alpha_{23} and α13\alpha_{13} are both zero.

Step 2.

By smoothing together α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2}, we deduce that α1=α2\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}.

Step 3.

By shifting mass between the variables αA\alpha_{A} with |A|=1|A|=1, we reduce to one of the following two situations. Either α1=α2=0\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=0, or 0<α1=α2=α3−α120<\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=\alpha_{3}-\alpha_{12}.

Step 4.

We solve the first case resulting from Step 3, which is vastly simpler than the original problem. We find that the solution corresponds to outcomes (i) and (ii) of Proposition 4.10.

Step 5.

It remains to consider the second case resulting from Step 3. By taking mass away from both α123\alpha_{123} and α1\alpha_{1}, and giving it to α12\alpha_{12}, we conclude that α123=0\alpha_{123}=0.

Step 6.

We are left with the situation where the only nonzero variables are α1\alpha_{1}, α2\alpha_{2}, α3\alpha_{3}, and α12\alpha_{12}, and they are related by the equation α1=α2=α3−α12\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=\alpha_{3}-\alpha_{12}. Again, this is vastly simpler than the original problem, and we find that its solution corresponds to outcome (iii) of Proposition 4.10.

4.2.2 Details of solution

We begin by recording a simple result that we will use repeatedly in the solution.

Lemma 4.11.

Let 𝛂{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} be a vector that solves opt​(γ)\text{\sc opt}(\gamma). Then e​(𝛂)=γ\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\gamma. Furthermore, if 𝛂′{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\prime} is obtained from 𝛂{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} by shifting mass from some αA\alpha_{A} to another αB\alpha_{B} with |A|=|B||A|=|B|, then e​(𝛂′)≤e​(𝛂)\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\prime})\leq\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}).

Proof.  Suppose for contradiction that e​(𝜶)>γ\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})>\gamma. The slack in the edge constraint lets us shift some more mass to α123\alpha_{123} while keeping e​(𝜶)≥γ\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq\gamma. But in the definition of obj, the coefficient (log⁡3\log 3) of α123\alpha_{123} is the largest, so this shift strictly increases obj, contradicting maximality of 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}.

For the second claim, observe that obj is invariant under the shift since |A|=|B||A|=|B|. Now suppose for contradiction that e​(𝜶′)>e​(𝜶)\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\prime})>\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}). Then, as above, we could shift more mass to α123\alpha_{123}, which would strictly increase obj, again contradicting the maximality of 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}. □\Box

Step 1.  Consider shifting mass among {α12,α23,α13}\{\alpha_{12},\alpha_{23},\alpha_{13}\}. If we hold all other αA\alpha_{A} constant, then e​(𝜶)=α1​α23+α2​α13+α3​α12+constant\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\alpha_{1}\alpha_{23}+\alpha_{2}\alpha_{13}+\alpha_{3}\alpha_{12}+\text{constant}, which is linear in the three variables of interest.

Let us postpone the uniqueness claim for a moment. Since we ordered α1≤α2≤α3\alpha_{1}\leq\alpha_{2}\leq\alpha_{3}, shifting all of the mass from {α13,α23}\{\alpha_{13},\alpha_{23}\} to α12\alpha_{12} will either strictly grow e​(𝜶)\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) if α2<α3\alpha_{2}<\alpha_{3}, or keep e​(𝜶)\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) unchanged. Also, obj​(𝜶)\text{\sc obj}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) will be invariant. Therefore, if we are only looking for an upper bound for opt​(γ)\text{\sc opt}(\gamma), we may perform this shift, and reduce to the case when α13=0=α23\alpha_{13}=0=\alpha_{23} without loss of generality.

We return to the topic of uniqueness. The next five steps of this solution will deduce that, conditioned on α13=0=α23\alpha_{13}=0=\alpha_{23}, the unique optimal 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} always has either α2<α3\alpha_{2}<\alpha_{3} or α12=α13=α23=0\alpha_{12}=\alpha_{13}=\alpha_{23}=0. We claim that this implies that our initial shift of mass to α12\alpha_{12} never happened. Indeed, in the case with α2<α3\alpha_{2}<\alpha_{3}, the previous paragraph shows that an initial shift would have strictly increased e​(𝜶)\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}), violating Lemma 4.11. And in the case with α12=α13=α23=0\alpha_{12}=\alpha_{13}=\alpha_{23}=0, there was not even any mass at all to shift. Therefore, this will imply the full uniqueness result.

Step 2.  Consider shifting mass between α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2} until they become equal. If we hold all other αA\alpha_{A} constant, then e​(𝜶)=α1​α2+(α1+α2)​α3+constant\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}+(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})\alpha_{3}+\text{constant}. This “smoothing” operation strictly increases the first term, while keeping the other terms invariant. But Lemma 4.11 prohibits e​(𝜶)\text{\sc e}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) from increasing, so we conclude that we must have had α1=α2\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}.

Step 3.  Consider shifting mass among {α1,α2,α3}\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3}\}. That is, fix S=α1+α2+α3S=\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3}, and vary t=α3t=\alpha_{3} in the range 0≤t≤S0\leq t\leq S. By Step 2, α1=α2=S−t2\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=\frac{S-t}{2}. =\displaystyle= −34​t2+(S2+α12)​t+S24.\displaystyle-\frac{3}{4}t^{2}+\left(\frac{S}{2}+\alpha_{12}\right)t+\frac{S^{2}}{4}.

Step 4.  In this case, only α3\alpha_{3}, α12\alpha_{12}, and α123\alpha_{123} are nonzero. x,y≥0,x+y≤1,x​y=γ.x,y\geq 0,\quad\quad x+y\leq 1,\quad\quad xy=\gamma.

Indeed, suppose for the sake of contradiction that α123>0\alpha_{123}>0.
