5 Exact result for sparse graphs

In this section, we determine the precise structure of the sparse graphs that maximize the number of colorings, completing the proof of Theorem 1.2. Proposition 3.6(ii) showed that in this regime, the optimal graphs were close, in edit distance, to complete bipartite graphs. As a warm-up for the arguments that will follow in this section, let us begin by showing that the semi-complete subgraphs of Definition 1.1 are optimal among bipartite graphs. We will use this in the final stage of our proof of the exact result.

Lemma 5.1.

Let q≥3q\geq 3 and r<a≤br<a\leq b be positive integers. Among all subgraphs of Ka,bK_{a,b} with rr missing edges, the ones which maximize the number of qq-colorings are precisely:

(i)

both the correctly and incorrectly oriented semi-complete subgraphs, when q=3q=3, and

(ii)

the correctly oriented semi-complete subgraph, when q≥4q\geq 4 and ba≥log⁡q/log⁡q−2q−3\frac{b}{a}\geq\log q/\log\frac{q-2}{q-3} and aa is sufficiently large (i.e., a>Nqa>N_{q}, where NqN_{q} depends only on qq).

Remark.  The above result is not as clean when more than 3 colors are used, but is sufficient for our purposes. In the sparse case, we encounter only highly unbalanced bipartite graphs, all of which have part size ratio approximately log⁡q/log⁡qq−1\log q/\log\frac{q}{q-1}. Apparently out of sheer coincidence (and good fortune), this is just barely enough to satisfy the additional condition of the lemma. Nevertheless, it would be nice to remove that condition.

Proof of Lemma 5.1(ii).  Let A∪BA\cup B be the vertex partition of Ka,bK_{a,b}, with |A|=a|A|=a and |B|=b|B|=b. Let F∗F^{*} be the correctly oriented semi-complete subgraph of Ka,bK_{a,b} with exactly rr missing edges. Let FF be another non-isomorphic subgraph of Ka,bK_{a,b} with the same number of edges. We will show that FF has fewer colorings. Since FF and F∗F^{*} are both bipartite, they share every coloring that uses a different set of colors on each side of the bipartition. Discrepancies arise when the same color appears on both sides. Note, however, that whenever this occurs, every edge between same-colored vertices must be missing from the graph. This set of forced missing edges,66 6 In this lemma, missing edges refer only to those missing from the bipartite Ka,bK_{a,b}, not the entire Ka+bK_{a+b}. which we call the coloring’s footprint, is always a union of vertex-disjoint complete bipartite graphs, one per color that appears on both sides. For each subset HH of the missing edges of FF, let nHn_{H} be the number of colorings of FF with footprint HH. Then, ∑nH\sum n_{H} is exactly the number of colorings of FF. To give each nHn_{H} a counterpart from F∗F^{*}, fix an arbitrary bijection ϕ\phi between the missing edges of FF and F∗F^{*}, and let nH∗n_{H}^{*} be the number of colorings of F∗F^{*} with footprint ϕ⁡(H)\phi(H). Since F∗F^{*} has ∑nH∗\sum n_{H}^{*} colorings, it suffices to show that nH≤nH∗n_{H}\leq n_{H}^{*} for all HH, with strict inequality for at least one HH.

Clearly, when HH is empty, or a star centered in BB, then nH=nH∗n_{H}=n_{H}^{*}. We observed that all footprints are unions Γ1∪⋯∪Γk\Gamma_{1}\cup\cdots\cup\Gamma_{k} of vertex-disjoint complete bipartite graphs, so all HH not of that form automatically have nH=0<nH∗n_{H}=0<n_{H}^{*}. It remains to consider HH that have this form, but are not stars centered in BB. Colorings with this footprint are monochromatic on each Γi\Gamma_{i}, and there are (qk)​k!{q\choose k}k! ways to choose a distinct color for each Γi\Gamma_{i}. The remaining q−kq-k colors are partitioned into two sets, one for A∖V⁡(H)A\setminus V(H) and one for B∖V⁡(H)B\setminus V(H). Crucially, |B∖V⁡(H)|≤b−2|B\setminus V(H)|\leq b-2 because HH is not a star centered in BB. Thus,

nH\displaystyle n_{H} ≤\displaystyle\leq [(qk)​k!]⋅∑i=1q−k−1(q−ki)​i|A∖V⁡(H)|​(q−k−i)|B∖V⁡(H)|\displaystyle\left[{q\choose k}k!\right]\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{q-k-1}{q-k\choose i}i^{|A\setminus V(H)|}(q-k-i)^{|B\setminus V(H)|}
≤\displaystyle\leq qk⋅∑i=1q−k−1(q−ki)​ia​(q−k−i)b−2.\displaystyle q^{k}\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{q-k-1}{q-k\choose i}i^{a}(q-k-i)^{b-2}.

To see that the sum is dominated by the i=1i=1 term, note that since we assumed that ba≥log⁡q/log⁡q−2q−3\frac{b}{a}\geq\log q/\log\frac{q-2}{q-3}, for sufficiently large aa we have

b−2a≥log⁡(q−1)/log⁡q−2q−3≥log⁡(q−k)/log⁡q−k−1q−k−2,\frac{b-2}{a}\geq\log(q-1)/\log\frac{q-2}{q-3}\geq\log(q-k)/\log\frac{q-k-1}{q-k-2},

so we may apply Inequality B.2(ii). This gives nH≤qk⋅1.1​(q−k)​(q−k−1)b−2n_{H}\leq q^{k}\cdot 1.1(q-k)(q-k-1)^{b-2}. Next, we claim that this bound is greatest when kk is smallest. Indeed, when kk increases by one, qkq^{k} increases by the factor qq, but (q−k−1)b−2(q-k-1)^{b-2} decreases by a factor of at least (q−2q−3)b−2≫q\big(\frac{q-2}{q-3}\big)^{b-2}\gg q for large bb. Hence we have nH≤1.1​q​(q−1)​(q−2)b−2n_{H}\leq 1.1q(q-1)(q-2)^{b-2}.

On the other hand, ϕ⁡(H)\phi(H) is always a star centered in BB, so we can easily construct q⁡(q−1)​(q−2)b−1q(q-1)(q-2)^{b-1} colorings of F∗F^{*}. Indeed, choose one color for the vertices of the graph ϕ⁡(H)\phi(H), a different color for the remainder of A∖ϕ⁡(H)A\setminus\phi(H), and allow each vertex left in B∖ϕ⁡(H)B\setminus\phi(H) to take any of the other q−2q-2 colors. Since ϕ⁡(H)\phi(H) intersects BB in exactly one vertex, nH∗≥q⁡(q−1)​(q−2)b−1n_{H}^{*}\geq q(q-1)(q-2)^{b-1}, as claimed. But q−2≥2q-2\geq 2, so we have the desired strict inequality nH∗≥2​q​(q−1)​(q−2)b−2>nHn_{H}^{*}\geq 2q(q-1)(q-2)^{b-2}>n_{H} for all remaining HH. □\Box

Part (i) is a consequence of the following more precise result, which we will also need later.

Lemma 5.2.

Let FF be a subgraph of the complete bipartite graph Ka,bK_{a,b} with vertex partition A∪BA\cup B, and r<max⁡{a,b}r<\max\{a,b\} missing edges. Suppose FF has x∈Ax\in A and y∈By\in B with xx complete to BB and yy complete to AA. Then its number of 3-colorings is precisely 3⋅2a+3⋅2b−6+6​s3\cdot 2^{a}+3\cdot 2^{b}-6+6s, where ss is the number of nonempty subsets of missing edges which form complete bipartite graphs. This is at most 3⋅2a+3⋅2b+6⋅(2r−2)3\cdot 2^{a}+3\cdot 2^{b}+6\cdot(2^{r}-2), with equality when the missing edges form a star.

Proof.  As in the proof of Lemma 5.1(ii), let nHn_{H} be the number of 3-colorings of FF with footprint HH. The key observation is that for every nonempty HH, nH=6n_{H}=6 when HH is a complete bipartite graph, and nH=0n_{H}=0 otherwise. Indeed, if HH is not a complete bipartite graph, then it cannot be a footprint of a 3-coloring, so nH=0n_{H}=0. Otherwise, there are 3 ways to choose a color for the vertices of HH, and then by definition of footprint, the remaining two colors must be split between A∖HA\setminus H and B∖HB\setminus H. Both of these sets are nonempty, because A∖HA\setminus H must contain the given vertex xx and B∖HB\setminus H must contain yy, so the only way to split the two colors is to use one on all of A∖HA\setminus H and the other on all of B∖HB\setminus H. There are 2 ways to decide how to do this. So, nH=3⋅2=6n_{H}=3\cdot 2=6, as claimed, and this produces the 6​s6s in the formula.

The rest of the formula follows from n∅=3⋅2a+3⋅2b−6n_{\emptyset}=3\cdot 2^{a}+3\cdot 2^{b}-6. Indeed, the terms correspond to the colorings that use a single color (for which there are three choices) on BB and allow the other two on AA, those that use one on AA and allow the others on BB, and those that use only one on each of AA and BB (hence were double-counted). The final claim in the statement comes from the fact that stars are the only rr-edge graphs which have all 2r−12^{r}-1 of their nonempty subgraphs complete bipartite. □\Box

Proof of Lemma 5.1(i).  Since the number of missing edges rr is less than both |A||A| and |B||B|, the vertices xx and yy of Lemma 5.2 must exist. Therefore, its equality condition implies that the optimal subgraphs are indeed semi-complete. □\Box

5.1 Structure of proof

We will use several small constants with relative order of magnitude ϵ1≪ϵ2≪ϵ3\epsilon_{1}\ll\epsilon_{2}\ll\epsilon_{3}, related by ϵ1=ϵ22=ϵ33\epsilon_{1}=\epsilon_{2}^{2}=\epsilon_{3}^{3}. We do not send them to zero; rather, we show that there is an eventual choice of the ϵi\epsilon_{i}, determined by qq and κ\kappa, that makes our argument work. So, to avoid confusion, the OO, Θ\Theta, and oo notation that we employ in this proof will only mask constants depending on q,κq,\kappa alone. For example, we will write X=O⁡(ϵ2​Y)X=O(\epsilon_{2}Y) when there is a constant Cq,κC_{q,\kappa} such that X≤Cq,κ​ϵ2​YX\leq C_{q,\kappa}\epsilon_{2}Y for sufficiently large mm and nn. Occasionally, we will use phrases like “almost all colorings have property PP” when (1−o⁡(1))(1-o(1))-fraction of all colorings have that property.

Proof of Theorem 1.2.  Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be an optimal graph with nn vertices and m≤κ​n2m\leq\kappa n^{2} edges. We begin with a convenient technical modification: if GG has an isolated edge x​yxy, replace it with an edge between xx and another non-isolated vertex of minimal degree. Do this only once, even if GG had multiple isolated edges. The number of colorings stays the same because both graphs share the same partial colorings of V∖{x}V\setminus\{x\}, and each of those has exactly q−1q-1 extensions (in each graph) to the degree-1 vertex xx.

This adjustment will not compromise the uniqueness claim, because it cannot create one of the optimal graphs listed in Theorem 1.2. Indeed, if it did, then the degree-1 vertex xx would now have to be the center of the missing star of the semi-complete subgraph H⊂Ka,b⊂GH\subset K_{a,b}\subset G. But we made xx adjacent to a vertex of minimal degree, so xx must be on the smaller side of HH’s bipartition. Then the number of Ka,bK_{a,b}-edges missing from the semi-complete HH is precisely b−d⁡(x)=b−1b-d(x)=b-1. This exceeds aa for all optimal graphs listed in Theorem 1.2, but our definition of semi-completeness required that the number of missing edges was strictly less than the size of the smaller part. This contradiction shows that we may assume without loss of generality that if GG has an isolated edge u​vuv, then it also contains a degree-1 vertex x∉{u,v}x\not\in\{u,v\}.

Define u1=m⋅log⁡qq−1/log⁡qu_{1}=\sqrt{m\cdot\log\frac{q}{q-1}/\log q} and u2=m⋅log⁡q/log⁡qq−1u_{2}=\sqrt{m\cdot\log q/\log\frac{q}{q-1}}, and note that u1u2=log⁡qq−1/log⁡q\frac{u_{1}}{u_{2}}=\log\frac{q}{q-1}/\log q and u1​u2=mu_{1}u_{2}=m. So, Proposition 3.6(ii) gives disjoint subsets U1,U2⊂VU_{1},U_{2}\subset V of size |Ui|=⌈ui⌉|U_{i}|=\lceil u_{i}\rceil, such that by editing at most ϵ1​m\epsilon_{1}m edges, we can transform GG into the complete bipartite graph between U1U_{1} and U2U_{2}, with all other vertices isolated. Call that graph G∗G^{*}.

Let (V1,V2)(V_{1},V_{2}) be a max-cut partition of the non-isolated vertices of GG, such that V1V_{1} contains at least as many vertices of U1U_{1} as V2V_{2} does. We would like to show that this partition is very close to (U1,U2)(U_{1},U_{2}), so we keep track of the UiU_{i} by defining Ui′=Ui∩ViU_{i}^{\prime}=U_{i}\cap V_{i} and Ui′′=Ui∩V3−iU_{i}^{\prime\prime}=U_{i}\cap V_{3-i} for each i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}. Claim 1.

For each ii, |Ui′||U_{i}^{\prime}| is within O⁡(ϵ1​m)O(\epsilon_{1}\sqrt{m}) of uiu_{i}, |Xi||X_{i}| is within O⁡(ϵ2​m)O(\epsilon_{2}\sqrt{m}) of uiu_{i}, and |Ui′′|≤O⁡(ϵ1​m)|U_{i}^{\prime\prime}|\leq O(\epsilon_{1}\sqrt{m}).

Crucially, log⁡q/log⁡qq−1\log q/\log\frac{q}{q-1} is always irrational, because any positive integral solution to qx=(qq−1)yq^{x}=\big(\frac{q}{q-1}\big)^{y} would require qq and q−1q-1 to have a nontrivial common factor. So, by choosing our ϵ\epsilon’s sufficiently small in advance (based only on qq), we may ensure that t≥log⁡q/log⁡qq−1−1+cqt\geq\log q/\log\frac{q}{q-1}-1+c_{q} for some small positive constant cqc_{q}. Since (qq−1)log⁡q/log⁡qq−1−1⋅1q−1=1\big(\frac{q}{q-1}\big)^{\log q/\log\frac{q}{q-1}-1}\cdot\frac{1}{q-1}=1, this gives Σ6/Σ5≥(1−o⁡(1))​(qq−1)cq\Sigma_{6}/\Sigma_{5}\geq(1-o(1))\big(\frac{q}{q-1}\big)^{c_{q}}, which exceeds 1 for large mm, leaving G′G^{\prime} with more colorings than GG. This contradiction finishes our last case, and our entire proof. □\Box

6 Exact result for 3 colors

Our arguments can be pushed further when only three colors are used. In this section, we complete the proof of Theorem 1.3, determining the precise structure of the graphs that maximize the number of 3-colorings, for edge densities up to m≤14​n2m\leq\frac{1}{4}n^{2} (i.e., up to the density of the complete bipartite graph). The structure of this proof closely resembles that of the previous section, so parts that are essentially the same are rewritten briefly.

We would, however, like to draw attention to a new piece of notation. Recall that, as defined in the previous section, a coloring is (X,Y)(X,Y)-regular if it uses only one color on XX and the other q−1q-1 on YY. This time, we will also need a symmetric version of this concept, which we denote with square brackets. We will say that a coloring is [X,Y][X,Y]-regular if one of XX or YY is monochromatic, and the other uses only the other two colors.

Proof of Theorem 1.3.  Theorem 1.2 already established our result for densities up to m≤κ​n2m\leq\kappa n^{2} for some constant κ\kappa, so we may assume that m=Θ⁡(n2)m=\Theta(n^{2}). Routine algebra verifies that Proposition 4.10 and Theorem 3.2 establish the claimed numbers of colorings in this theorem. This leaves us to concentrate on the optimal graph structure. We use several constants ϵ1≪ϵ2≪ϵ3\epsilon_{1}\ll\epsilon_{2}\ll\epsilon_{3}, related by ϵ1=ϵ22=ϵ33\epsilon_{1}=\epsilon_{2}^{2}=\epsilon_{3}^{3}, and show that there is an eventual choice that makes our argument work. To avoid confusion, our OO, Θ\Theta, and oo notation will only mask constants determined by qq alone.

Let u1=α3​nu_{1}=\alpha_{3}n and u2=α12​nu_{2}=\alpha_{12}n, where the α\alpha’s are determined by Proposition 4.10 with density parameter γ=m/n2\gamma=m/n^{2}. Theorem 3.3 gives disjoint subsets U1,U2⊂VU_{1},U_{2}\subset V with |Ui|∈{⌊ui⌋,⌈ui⌉}|U_{i}|\in\{\lfloor u_{i}\rfloor,\lceil u_{i}\rceil\}, such that by editing at most ϵ1​n2\epsilon_{1}n^{2} edges, we can transform GG into the complete bipartite graph between U1U_{1} and U2U_{2}, plus isolated vertices. Since G′G^{\prime} is complete bipartite, it has exactly 3⋅2s+3⋅2n−s−63\cdot 2^{s}+3\cdot 2^{n-s}-6 colorings, and thus our bound on ss implies that G′G^{\prime} has strictly more than 3⋅2s≥3⋅2|V2∗|−⌈t⌉3\cdot 2^{s}\geq 3\cdot 2^{|V_{2}^{*}|-\lceil\sqrt{t}\rceil} colorings. Yet for t≥3t\geq 3, one may check that −⌈t⌉≥(−2​t+1)+0.4-\lceil\sqrt{t}\rceil\geq(-2\sqrt{t}+1)+0.4, giving G′G^{\prime} more colorings than GG, which is impossible.

We are left with the cases t∈{1,2}t\in\{1,2\}, but for these values there is always a vertex y∈V2∗y\in V_{2}^{*} with exactly 1 neighbor zz in G⁡[V2∗]G[V_{2}^{*}]. This forces all edges to be present between the Vi∗V_{i}^{*}, because otherwise we could increase the number of (V1∗,V2∗)(V_{1}^{*},V_{2}^{*})-regular colorings by a factor of 2 by deleting the edge y​zyz and adding one of the missing edges between the Vi∗V_{i}^{*}. The presence of the complete bipartite graph forces every coloring of GG to use exactly two colors on V2∗V_{2}^{*}, and the other on V1∗V_{1}^{*}. Together with the observation that the maximum number of connected components of G⁡[V2∗]G[V_{2}^{*}] is |V2∗|−t|V_{2}^{*}|-t when t∈{1,2}t\in\{1,2\}, we find that GG has exactly 3⋅2r≤3⋅2|V2∗|−t3\cdot 2^{r}\leq 3\cdot 2^{|V_{2}^{*}|-t} colorings. On the other hand, we showed above that G′G^{\prime} had more than 3⋅2|V2∗|−⌈t⌉3\cdot 2^{|V_{2}^{*}|-\lceil\sqrt{t}\rceil} colorings. Since t=⌈t⌉t=\lceil\sqrt{t}\rceil for t∈{1,2}t\in\{1,2\}, G′G^{\prime} has more colorings than GG, contradiction. □\Box

Proof of Claim 6.  Let G0=G⁡[V1∪V2]G_{0}=G[V_{1}\cup V_{2}] be the graph formed by the non-isolated vertices of GG, and let n0=|V1∪V2|n_{0}=|V_{1}\cup V_{2}|. 7 Exact result for Turán graphs

We now study the extremality of Turán graphs. As we mentioned in the introduction, Lazebnik conjectured that Turán graphs Tr​(n)T_{r}(n) were the unique graphs that maximized the number of qq-colorings whenever r≤qr\leq q. Note that Theorem 1.3 implies this result for q=3q=3 and r=2r=2 when nn is large, because it shows that all optimal graphs are bipartite, and no other bipartite graph has as many edges as T2​(n)T_{2}(n). In this section, we prove Theorem 1.4, which confirms (for large nn) Lazebnik’s conjecture when r=q−1r=q-1, for all remaining qq. Our proof relies on the following special case of a result of Simonovits [27]. Let tr​(n)t_{r}(n) denote the number of edges of the rr-partite Turán graph Tr​(n)T_{r}(n) with nn vertices.

Fact 7.1.

Let FF be a graph with chromatic number r+1r+1. Suppose there is an edge whose deletion makes FF rr-colorable. Then for all sufficiently large nn, the Turán graph Tr​(n)T_{r}(n) is the unique nn-vertex graph with at least tr​(n)t_{r}(n) edges that does not contain a subgraph isomorphic to FF.

We use this fact to prove the following lemma, which we will need later.

Lemma 7.1.

Let q≥4q\geq 4 be fixed. The following holds for all sufficiently large nn. Let G≠Tq−1​(n)G\neq T_{q-1}(n) have nn vertices, and at least as many edges and qq-colorings as Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n). Let Δ\Delta be the difference between the number of edges of GG and Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n), and let n′=n−(q−1)n^{\prime}=n-(q-1). Then there is an n′n^{\prime}-vertex graph HH with at least Δ+1\Delta+1 more edges than Tq−1​(n′)T_{q-1}(n^{\prime}), and at least half as many qq-colorings as GG.

Proof.  We begin with a convenient technical adjustment. If GG has k≥2k\geq 2 connectivity components CiC_{i} that are not isolated vertices, then choose vertices vi∈Civ_{i}\in C_{i} and glue the components together by merging all of the viv_{i} into a single vertex vv. Add k−1k-1 isolated vertices w1,…,wk−1w_{1},\ldots,w_{k-1} to restore the vertex count, and let G′G^{\prime} be the resulting graph. Clearly, G′G^{\prime} has as many edges as GG, and it also is not Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n) because G′G^{\prime} has a vertex whose deletion increases the number of components while Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n) does not. Furthermore, we claim that GG and G′G^{\prime} have the same number of colorings. Indeed, by symmetry, for an arbitrary color cc, the total number of colorings of GG is precisely qkq^{k} times the number of colorings of GG which use cc for every viv_{i}. The obvious correspondence gives a bijection between these colorings and partial colorings of G′∖{w1,…,wk−1}G^{\prime}\setminus\{w_{1},\ldots,w_{k-1}\} which use cc on the merged vertex vv. Yet the wiw_{i} are isolated, so each of these partial colorings has exactly qk−1q^{k-1} extensions to all of G′G^{\prime}. Again by symmetry, the total number of colorings of G′G^{\prime} is precisely qq times the number that use cc on vv. Putting everything together, we find that GG and G′G^{\prime} indeed have the same number of colorings. Therefore, by replacing GG with G′G^{\prime}, we may assume without loss of generality that GG has only one nontrivial connectivity component.

Fact 7.1 implies that for large nn, GG has a subgraph FF which is the complete (q−1)(q-1)-partite graph on V⁡(F)=X1∪…∪Xq−1V(F)=X_{1}\cup\ldots\cup X_{q-1} with each part Xi={ui,wi}X_{i}=\{u_{i},w_{i}\} consisting of two vertices, plus an extra edge u1​w1u_{1}w_{1}. Let UU and WW be the sets of the {ui}\{u_{i}\} and {wi}\{w_{i}\}, respectively, and let A=U∪{w1}A=U\cup\{w_{1}\}.

Let δ\delta be the difference between the number of edges of Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n) and Tq−1​(n′)T_{q-1}(n^{\prime}). We claim that if there is a set YY of q−1q-1 vertices of AA such that the sum of their degrees is at most δ+(q−12)−1\delta+{q-1\choose 2}-1, then H=G−YH=G-Y satisfies the lemma’s assertion. Clearly, HH has the correct number of vertices, and it has the correct number of edges because Y⊂AY\subset A induces a complete graph Kq−1K_{q-1}, so the number of deleted edges is at most δ−1\delta-1. We now show that every qq-coloring of HH extends to at most two qq-colorings of GG.

If Y=UY=U, since {u1}∪W\{u_{1}\}\cup W induces a KqK_{q}-subgraph in GG, every coloring of H⊃WH\supset W has at most 1 extension to u1u_{1}. Then, every other uiu_{i} has at most 1 choice because {u1,ui}∪(W∖{wi})\{u_{1},u_{i}\}\cup(W\setminus\{w_{i}\}) induces a KqK_{q}-subgraph in which uiu_{i} is the only uncolored vertex. Thus when Y=UY=U, every coloring of HH colors WW and hence has at most 1 extension to GG. On the other hand, up to a symmetry of FF, the only other case is when Y={w1}∪(U∖{uq−1})Y=\{w_{1}\}\cup(U\setminus\{u_{q-1}\}). As before, {u1}∪W\{u_{1}\}\cup W induces a KqK_{q}-subgraph in GG, but this time HH contains neither u1u_{1} nor w1w_{1} (although it contains the rest). Any partial coloring of q−2q-2 vertices of KqK_{q} has only 2 completions, so there are at most 2 ways to extend any coloring of HH to include u1u_{1} and w1w_{1}. But then every other uiu_{i} has at most 1 choice because {u1,ui}∪(W∖{wi})\{u_{1},u_{i}\}\cup(W\setminus\{w_{i}\}) induces a KqK_{q}-subgraph in which uiu_{i} is the only uncolored vertex. Therefore, every coloring of HH has at most 2 extensions to GG, as claimed.

It remains to consider the case when every set of q−1q-1 vertices of AA has degrees summing to at least δ+(q−12)\delta+{q-1\choose 2}. We will show that then GG has fewer colorings than Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n), which is impossible. Let B=V⁡(G)∖AB=V(G)\setminus A. By an averaging argument, the sum of degrees of AA is at least qq−1​[δ+(q−12)]\frac{q}{q-1}\big[\delta+{q-1\choose 2}\big]. Since |A|=q|A|=q, the number of edges between AA and BB is at least qq−1​[δ+(q−12)]−2​(q2)\frac{q}{q-1}\big[\delta+{q-1\choose 2}\big]-2{q\choose 2}.

Let B0B_{0} be the set of isolated vertices of GG, and for 2≤i≤q−12\leq i\leq q-1, let BiB_{i} be the set of vertices of BB that send ii edges to AA. Note that no vertex can send q=|A|q=|A| edges to AA because that would create a Kq+1K_{q+1}-subgraph, making GG not qq-colorable. So, if we let B1=B∖(B0∪B2∪⋯∪Bq−1)B_{1}=B\setminus(B_{0}\cup B_{2}\cup\cdots\cup B_{q-1}), then every vertex of B1B_{1} either sends exactly 1 edge to AA, or it is a non-isolated vertex that sends no edges to AA. Let bi=|Bi|b_{i}=|B_{i}|. By counting the number of edges between AA and BB, we obtain:

∑i=1q−1i​bi≥qq−1​[δ+(q−12)]−2​(q2).\sum_{i=1}^{q-1}ib_{i}\ \ \geq\ \ \frac{q}{q-1}\left[\delta+{q-1\choose 2}\right]-2{q\choose 2}. (4)

We now bound the number of qq-colorings of GG in terms of the bib_{i}. There are exactly q!q! ways to color AA because it induces KqK_{q}. Then, there are exactly qb0q^{b_{0}} ways to extend this partial coloring to B0B_{0} because each isolated vertex has a free choice of the qq colors. Next, for every i∈{2,…,q−1}i\in\{2,\ldots,q-1\}, each vertex in BiB_{i} has at most q−iq-i color choices left because it is adjacent to ii vertices in AA, all of which received different colors since G⁡[A]=KqG[A]=K_{q}. Finally, we color the vertices of B1B_{1} by considering them in an order such that whenever we color a vertex, it always has a neighbor that we already colored. This is possible because our initial technical adjustment allows us to assume that GG has only one nontrivial connectivity component. Hence each vertex in B1B_{1} will have at most q−1q-1 choices. Putting this all together, we find that the number of qq-colorings of GG is at most

q!⋅∏i=0q−1(q−i)bi≤q!⋅∏i=0q−12(q−i−1)​bi≤q!⋅2(q−1)​(n−q)⋅2−qq−1​[δ+(q−12)]+2​(q2),q!\cdot\prod_{i=0}^{q-1}(q-i)^{b_{i}}\ \ \leq\ \ q!\cdot\prod_{i=0}^{q-1}2^{(q-i-1)b_{i}}\ \ \leq\ \ q!\cdot 2^{(q-1)(n-q)}\cdot 2^{-\frac{q}{q-1}\left[\delta+{q-1\choose 2}\right]+2{q\choose 2}},

where we used the inequality x+1≤2xx+1\leq 2^{x} for x∈ℤx\in\mathbb{Z}, the identity ∑bi=n−q\sum b_{i}=n-q (since ∪Bi=V⁡(G)∖A\cup B_{i}=V(G)\setminus A), and the bound for ∑i​bi\sum ib_{i} from inequality (4). Inequality B.5 routinely verifies that this final bound is always strictly less than the number of colorings of Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n), contradicting our assumption that GG had at least that many colorings. □\Box

Proof of Theorem 1.4.  Let q≥4q\geq 4 be fixed, and let NN be the corresponding minimum number of vertices for which Lemma 7.1 holds (it is valid only for sufficiently large nn). We will show that Theorem 1.4 holds for all n≥q​(N2)n\geq q{N\choose 2}. So, suppose for contradiction that G≠Tq−1​(n)G\neq T_{q-1}(n) is an nn-vertex graph with at least as many edges and qq-colorings as Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n).

Define a sequence of graphs as follows. Start with G0=GG_{0}=G. If GiG_{i} is the current graph, stop if GiG_{i} has fewer colorings than the (q−1)(q-1)-partite Turán graph with n−(q−1)​in-(q-1)i vertices. Otherwise, let Gi+1G_{i+1} be the graph HH obtained by applying Lemma 7.1 to GiG_{i}. We claim that this process terminates before the graph GiG_{i} has fewer than NN vertices, so we will always be able to apply the lemma. Indeed, each GiG_{i} has exactly n−(q−1)​in-(q-1)i vertices, so it will take more than (N2){N\choose 2} iterations before GiG_{i} has fewer than NN vertices. Yet if Δ≥0\Delta\geq 0 is the difference between the number of edges of GG and Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n), then each GiG_{i} has at least Δ+i\Delta+i more edges than the (q−1)(q-1)-partite Turán graph with n−(q−1)​in-(q-1)i vertices. So, after (N2){N\choose 2} iterations, GiG_{i} would certainly have more than the maximum number of edges of an NN-vertex graph, and we indeed can never reach a graph with fewer than NN vertices.

Therefore, we stop at some GtG_{t}, which has n′=n−(q−1)​tn^{\prime}=n-(q-1)t vertices and fewer colorings than Tq−1​(n′)T_{q-1}(n^{\prime}), but at least 2−t2^{-t} times as many colorings as GG. Divide nn by q−1q-1, so that n=s⁡(q−1)+rn=s(q-1)+r with 0≤r<q−10\leq r<q-1, and note that n′=(s−t)​(q−1)+rn^{\prime}=(s-t)(q-1)+r. Lemma B.4 calculates that Tq−1​(n′)T_{q-1}(n^{\prime}) has exactly q!⋅[(q−1+r)​2s−t−1−q+2]q!\cdot\big[(q-1+r)2^{s-t-1}-q+2\big] colorings, so GG has at most 2t2^{t} times that many, hence fewer than q!⋅[(q−1+r)​2s−1−q+2]q!\cdot\big[(q-1+r)2^{s-1}-q+2\big]. Yet by the same lemma, that final bound equals the number of colorings of Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n). Thus GG has fewer colorings than Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n), contradiction. □\Box

8 Concluding remarks

  • •

    We have developed an approach that we hope future researchers can use to determine the graphs that maximize the number of qq-colorings. Theorems 3.2 and 3.3 reduce any instance of this problem to a quadratically-constrained linear program, which can be solved for any case of interest. Thus, thanks to modern computer algebra packages, these theorems imply that for any fixed qq, approximately determining the extremal graphs amounts to a finite symbolic computation.

    The remaining challenge is to find analytic arguments which solve the optimization problem for general qq, and then refine the approximate structure into precise results. We accomplished this for low densities m/n2m/n^{2}, and the natural next step would be to extend the result to the range mn2≤14\frac{m}{n^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{4}. In this range, and for all qq, we expect the solution to the optimization problem to correspond to a bipartite graph plus isolated vertices. This common form gives hope that perhaps one can find a solution which works across all qq.

  • •

    For q=3q=3, we also know the approximate form of the extremal graphs when mn2>14\frac{m}{n^{2}}>\frac{1}{4}, since Proposition 4.10 solved the entire q=3q=3 case of the optimization problem. However, we did not pursue the precise structure of the optimal graphs because it appears that their description is substantially more involved, and this paper was already quite long.

  • •

    Our methods in Section 3 can easily be adapted to maximize the number of graph homomorphisms to an arbitrary HH (not just KqK_{q}). The analogues of Theorems 3.2 and 3.3 show that for any fixed HH, the asymptotic maximum number of homomorphisms from an nn-vertex, mm-edge graph to HH can be determined by solving a certain quadratically-constrained linear program. Although this can in principle be done, it appears that the computations become rather messy even for graphs HH of small order.

    However, in the interesting case when HH is the two-vertex graph consisting of a single edge plus a loop, one can easily determine the extremal graphs via a direct argument. As we mentioned in the introduction, this corresponds to maximizing the number of independent sets. By considering the complement of the graph, this is equivalent to maximizing the number of cliques.

    We claim that for any n,mn,m, the same graph that Linial found to minimize the number of colorings also happens to maximize the number of cliques. This graph G∗G^{*} was a clique KkK_{k} with an additional vertex adjacent to ll vertices of the KkK_{k}, plus n−k−1n-k-1 isolated vertices, where k,lk,l are the unique integers satisfying m=(k2)+lm={k\choose 2}+l with k>l≥0k>l\geq 0. We will show that for any tt, every nn-vertex graph GG with mm edges has at most as many tt-cliques as G∗G^{*}. The only nontrivial values of tt to check are 2≤t≤k2\leq t\leq k.

    If l+2≤t≤kl+2\leq t\leq k, then G∗G^{*} has exactly (kt){k\choose t} cliques of size tt. Suppose for contradiction that GG has more tt-cliques. Construct a tt-uniform hypergraph with at least (kt)+1=(kt)+(t−1t−1){k\choose t}+1={k\choose t}+{t-1\choose t-1} hyperedges by defining a hyperedge for each tt-clique. By the Kruskal-Katona theorem (see, e.g., the book [5]), the number of 2-sets that are contained in some hyperedge is at least (k2)+(t−11)≥(k2)+(l+1){k\choose 2}+{t-1\choose 1}\geq{k\choose 2}+(l+1), which exceeds the number of edges of GG. This contradicts the definition of the hyperedges, because each of these 2-sets must be an edge of GG.

    On the other hand, if 2≤t≤l+12\leq t\leq l+1, G∗G^{*} has exactly (kt)+(lt−1){k\choose t}+{l\choose t-1} cliques of size tt. A similar argument shows that if GG has at least (kt)+(lt−1)+1=(kt)+(lt−1)+(t−2t−2){k\choose t}+{l\choose t-1}+1={k\choose t}+{l\choose t-1}+{t-2\choose t-2} cliques of size tt, then GG must have at least (k2)+(l1)+(t−20)≥(k2)+l+1{k\choose 2}+{l\choose 1}+{t-2\choose 0}\geq{k\choose 2}+l+1 edges, contradiction.

    Therefore, G∗G^{*} indeed maximizes the number of cliques. Our argument also shows that any other maximizer has as many tt-cliques as G∗G^{*}, for every tt. It is not difficult to show that this implies the maximizer is unique unless l=1l=1, in which case the extremal graphs are KkK_{k} plus an arbitrary edge (not necessarily incident to the KkK_{k}).

The monotonicity of Fq​(x)F_{q}(x) on 0<x<q/20<x<q/2, which we just established, is useful for our next proof. This is Lemma 4.6, which stated that if 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} solves opt∗\text{\sc opt}^{*} and is supported by a partition of [q][q] consisting of exactly two sets, then 𝜶{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} must have the same form as 𝜶∗{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}, the claimed optimal vector in Proposition 4.1.

Proof of Lemma 4.6.  Let AA and BB denote the two sets in the support, with |A|≤|B||A|\leq|B|. Write a=|A|a=|A|. Flipping the fractions to make the logarithms positive, we have obj∗​(𝜶)=−αA​log⁡qa−αB​log⁡qq−a≤−2​αA​log⁡qa⋅αB​log⁡qq−a\text{\sc obj}^{*}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=-\alpha_{A}\log\frac{q}{a}-\alpha_{B}\log\frac{q}{q-a}\leq-2\sqrt{\alpha_{A}\log\frac{q}{a}\cdot\alpha_{B}\log\frac{q}{q-a}} by the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means. The remaining lemma from Section 4.1.3 ruled out a handful of partitions as possible supports for optimal vectors. It turns out that each of those excluded partitions is a special case of the following result.

Lemma A.1.

Proof of Lemma 4.7.  Part (i), the partition of all singletons, is precisely the case of the previous lemma when t=1t=1. Similarly, part (ii), the partition of all singletons except for a 2-set, corresponds to the t=2t=2 case. The only other possibility is that the partition is a (q−2)(q-2)-set plus a 2-set, and this is excluded by Lemma 4.6. □\Box

Appendix B Routine verifications for exact results

Proposition B.1.

Let rr be a sufficiently large positive integer. Then the complete bipartite graph Kr,2​rK_{r,2r} plus one pendant edge achieves the maximum number of colorings among all (3​r+1)(3r+1)-vertex graphs with 2​r2+12r^{2}+1 edges.

Proof.  Every 3-coloring of Kr,2​rK_{r,2r} has exactly 2 extensions to the pendant vertex, so Lemma 5.2 shows that the above graph has exactly (3⋅2r+3⋅22​r−6)⋅2=(1+o⁡(1))⋅3⋅22​r+1\big(3\cdot 2^{r}+3\cdot 2^{2r}-6\big)\cdot 2=(1+o(1))\cdot 3\cdot 2^{2r+1} colorings. Plugging n=3​r+1n=3r+1 and m=2​r2+1m=2r^{2}+1 into the dense case of Theorem 1.3, we see that the only other graphs we need to consider are semi-complete subgraphs of some Ka,bK_{a,b} with a=(1+o⁡(1))​ra=(1+o(1))r and b=(2+o⁡(1))​rb=(2+o(1))r, plus isolated vertices. Note that we must have a≥ra\geq r, because when a≤r−1a\leq r-1 and a+b≤3​r+1a+b\leq 3r+1, convexity implies that a​b≤(r−1)​(2​r+2)=2​r2−2<2​r2+1ab\leq(r-1)(2r+2)=2r^{2}-2<2r^{2}+1, and there would not be enough edges.

Let G′G^{\prime} be one of the above graphs with a=r+ta=r+t for some t≥0t\geq 0. We must have b≥2​r−2​t+1b\geq 2r-2t+1, because (r+t)​(2​r−2​t)=2​r2−2​t2<2​r2+1(r+t)(2r-2t)=2r^{2}-2t^{2}<2r^{2}+1, so any smaller bb would not produce enough edges. This leaves n−a−b≤tn-a-b\leq t isolated vertices. Observe that when t=0t=0, this forces G′G^{\prime} to be a semi-complete subgraph of Kr,2​r+1K_{r,2r+1} with exactly r−1r-1 missing edges. Lemma 5.2 then shows that the number of colorings of G′G^{\prime} is 3⋅2r+3⋅22​r+1+6⋅(2r−1−2)3\cdot 2^{r}+3\cdot 2^{2r+1}+6\cdot\big(2^{r-1}-2\big), which is exactly the same as GG.

It remains to consider t>0t>0. By definition, any semi-complete subgraph of Ka,bK_{a,b} is missing at most a−1a-1 edges, so Lemma 5.2 implies that the number of 3-colorings of G′G^{\prime} is at most 3n−a−b⋅(3⋅2a+3⋅2b+6⋅(2a−1−2))3^{n-a-b}\cdot\big(3\cdot 2^{a}+3\cdot 2^{b}+6\cdot\big(2^{a-1}-2\big)\big). This expression is largest when bb is as small as possible, so using b≥2​r−2​t+1b\geq 2r-2t+1 and n=3​r+1n=3r+1, we find that G′G^{\prime} has at most 3t⋅(3⋅2a+3⋅22​r−2​t+1+6⋅(2a−1−2))3^{t}\cdot\big(3\cdot 2^{a}+3\cdot 2^{2r-2t+1}+6\cdot\big(2^{a-1}-2\big)\big) colorings. Since a=(1+o⁡(1))​ra=(1+o(1))r, this is at most ((34)t+o⁡(1))⋅3⋅22​r+1\big(\big(\frac{3}{4}\big)^{t}+o(1)\big)\cdot 3\cdot 2^{2r+1}, which is indeed less than the number of colorings of GG when rr is large. □\Box

Remark.  A similar argument shows that for any c∈{0,±1,±2}c\in\{0,\pm 1,\pm 2\} and large rr, Kr,2​r+cK_{r,2r+c} plus a pendant edge is optimal among graphs with 3​r+c+13r+c+1 vertices and r⁡(2​r+c)+1r(2r+c)+1 edges. Interestingly enough, it can also be shown that these values of n,mn,m are the only ones which produce optimal graphs that are not semi-complete plus isolated vertices, when n,mn,m are large.

Inequality B.2.

Let a,b,ta,b,t be positive integers, with t≥3t\geq 3 and ba≥log⁡t/log⁡t−1t−2\frac{b}{a}\geq\log t/\log\frac{t-1}{t-2}. Then:

(i)

The product ia​(t−i)bi^{a}(t-i)^{b} falls by a factor of at least 1.5a1.5^{a} when ii increases by 1, for all i∈{1,…,t−2}i\in\{1,\ldots,t-2\}.

(ii)

If we further assume that aa is sufficiently large (depending only on tt), then ∑i=1t−1(ti)​ia​(t−i)b≤1.1⋅t​(t−1)b\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}{t\choose i}i^{a}(t-i)^{b}\leq 1.1\cdot t(t-1)^{b}, i.e., the first summand dominates.

Proof.  When i∈{1,…,t−2}i\in\{1,\ldots,t-2\} increases by 1, ii grows by a factor of at most 2, but t−it-i falls by at least t−1t−2\frac{t-1}{t-2}. Thus, the product ia​(t−i)bi^{a}(t-i)^{b} falls by a factor of at least (12)a​(t−1t−2)b=(12⋅(t−1t−2)b/a)a≥(12⋅t)a\big(\frac{1}{2}\big)^{a}\big(\frac{t-1}{t-2}\big)^{b}=\big(\frac{1}{2}\cdot\big(\frac{t-1}{t-2}\big)^{b/a}\big)^{a}\geq\big(\frac{1}{2}\cdot t\big)^{a}. Since t≥3t\geq 3, this gives (i).

For part (ii), when ii increases by 1, the term (ti){t\choose i} in the summand grows by a factor of at most tt, but by (i) the rest of the summand falls by a factor of at least 1.5a1.5^{a}. Thus for sufficiently large aa, each successive term of the sum falls by a factor of at least 1.4a>201.4^{a}>20. The result follows by bounding the sum by a geometric series, since 1+120+1202+⋯<1.11+\frac{1}{20}+\frac{1}{20^{2}}+\cdots<1.1. □\Box

Lemma B.4.

The number of qq-colorings of the Turán graph Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n) is exactly q!⋅[(q−1+r)​2s−1−q+2]q!\cdot\big[(q-1+r)2^{s-1}-q+2\big], where ss and rr are defined by n=s⁡(q−1)+rn=s(q-1)+r with 0≤r<q−10\leq r<q-1.

Proof.  The complete (q−1)(q-1)-partite graph Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n) has rr parts of size s+1s+1 and q−1−rq-1-r parts of size ss, and any qq-coloring must use different colors on each part. The number of qq-colorings that use exactly one color on each part is exactly q⋅(q−1)⋯2=q!q\cdot(q-1)\cdots 2=q!. All other colorings use 2 colors on one part, and one color on each of the other parts. There are (q2){q\choose 2} ways to choose which two colors are paired. If the pair of colors is used on one of the rr parts of size s+1s+1, then there are 2s+1−22^{s+1}-2 ways to color that part with exactly 2 colors, followed by (q−2)!(q-2)! ways to choose which color goes to each of the remaining parts. Otherwise, if the pair of colors appears on one of the q−1−rq-1-r parts of size ss, then there (2s−2)​(q−2)!(2^{s}-2)(q-2)! colorings of this form. Therefore, the number of qq-colorings of Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n) is exactly

q!+(q2)⋅[r⋅(2s+1−2)​(q−2)!+(q−1−r)⋅(2s−2)​(q−2)!]=q!⋅[(q−1+r)​2s−1−q+2],q!+{q\choose 2}\cdot\left[r\cdot(2^{s+1}-2)(q-2)!+(q-1-r)\cdot(2^{s}-2)(q-2)!\right]\ \ =\ \ q!\cdot\left[(q-1+r)2^{s-1}-q+2\right],

as claimed. □\Box

Inequality B.5.

Fix any q≥4q\geq 4. For all sufficiently large nn, the number of qq-colorings of the Turán graph Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n) is strictly greater than

q!⋅2(q−1)​(n−q)⋅2−qq−1​[δ+(q−12)]+2​(q2),q!\cdot 2^{(q-1)(n-q)}\cdot 2^{-\frac{q}{q-1}\left[\delta+{q-1\choose 2}\right]+2{q\choose 2}}, (5)

where δ\delta is the difference between the number of edges of Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n) and Tq−1​(n−q+1)T_{q-1}(n-q+1).

Proof.  Divide nn by q−1q-1, so that n=s⁡(q−1)+rn=s(q-1)+r with 0≤r<q−10\leq r<q-1. Then Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n) has exactly rr parts of size s+1s+1 and q−1−rq-1-r parts of size ss, and Tq−1​(n−q+1)T_{q-1}(n-q+1) is obtained by deleting one vertex per part. Each deleted vertex in a part of size s+1s+1 had degree n−s−1n-s-1, while each deleted vertex in a part of size ss had degree n−sn-s. Thus, the number of deleted edges is δ=r⁡(n−s−1)+(q−1−r)​(n−s)−(q−12)\delta=r(n-s-1)+(q-1-r)(n-s)-{q-1\choose 2}, where we had to subtract the double-counted edges of the Kq−1K_{q-1} induced by the set of deleted vertices. Substituting this into (5) and using n=s⁡(q−1)+rn=s(q-1)+r to simplify the expression, we obtain:

q!⋅2(q−1)​(n−q)⋅2−qq−1​[δ+(q−12)]+2​(q2)\displaystyle q!\cdot 2^{(q-1)(n-q)}\cdot 2^{-\frac{q}{q-1}\left[\delta+{q-1\choose 2}\right]+2{q\choose 2}} =\displaystyle= q!⋅2(q−1)​(n−q)⋅2−qq−1​[r⁡(n−s−1)+(q−1−r)​(n−s)]+2​(q2)\displaystyle q!\cdot 2^{(q-1)(n-q)}\cdot 2^{-\frac{q}{q-1}\left[r(n-s-1)+(q-1-r)(n-s)\right]+2{q\choose 2}}
=\displaystyle= q!⋅2s⋅2rq−1.\displaystyle q!\cdot 2^{s}\cdot 2^{\frac{r}{q-1}}.

It remains to show that this is strictly less than the number of colorings of Tq−1​(n)T_{q-1}(n), which Lemma B.4 calculated to be q!⋅[(q−1+r)​2s−1−q+2]=(1−o⁡(1))⋅q!⋅2s⋅q−1+r2q!\cdot\big[(q-1+r)2^{s-1}-q+2\big]=(1-o(1))\cdot q!\cdot 2^{s}\cdot\frac{q-1+r}{2}. Here, the o⁡(1)o(1) term tends to zero as nn grows (and s=⌊nq−1⌋s=\big\lfloor\frac{n}{q-1}\big\rfloor grows). Recall that 0≤r<q−10\leq r<q-1, so when r≥1r\geq 1 and q≥4q\geq 4 we always have 2rq−1<21≤q−1+r22^{\frac{r}{q-1}}<2^{1}\leq\frac{q-1+r}{2}, giving the desired result. On the other hand, when r=0r=0, the result follows from 2rq−1=20<32≤q−1+r22^{\frac{r}{q-1}}=2^{0}<\frac{3}{2}\leq\frac{q-1+r}{2}. □\Box
